obj.std-algebra.blade.formal: A \emph{$k$-blade} is an outer product $A = v_1 \wedge \dots \wedge v_k$ of $k$ vectors ($k \ge 1$); scalars are $0$-blades. The \emph{subspace} of a nonzero blade is $[A] = \{ x \in V : x \wedge A = 0 \}$. A nonzero $n$-blade is a \emph{pseudoscalar}.
obj.std-algebra.blade.technical: A blade is an outer product of vectors. A nonzero blade determines the subspace of vectors whose outer product with it vanishes; by \claimref{std-algebra.blade-subspace} this is the span of its factors, so blades stand for oriented, weighted subspaces.
obj.std-algebra.blade.lay: A blade is an oriented piece of a line, plane or higher flat, with a size. It is the algebra's way of holding a whole subspace as a single element.

credit.name: Claude Opus 5.5
credit.source: Co-Authored-By trailer of the commit that added it

obj.std-algebra.clifford-algebra.technical: The Clifford algebra of $(V, Q)$ is the associative unital algebra generated by the vectors of $V$ subject only to the rule that each vector squares to its quadratic form, $v^{2} = Q(v)$. "Subject only to" is made precise by the universal property: any linear map from $V$ into an associative algebra whose values square to $Q$ extends to exactly one algebra homomorphism. The product is the geometric product. $\Cl(p, q, r)$ is the algebra of the standard space of signature $(p, q, r)$.
obj.std-algebra.clifford-algebra.lay: The Clifford algebra lets you multiply arrows. The only rule imposed is that an arrow times itself is its square length, a plain number. Everything else, from complex numbers to rotations to spinors, follows from that single rule.

credit.name: Claude Opus 5.5
credit.source: Co-Authored-By trailer of the commit that added it

obj.std-algebra.clifford-conjugation.formal: \emph{Clifford conjugation} is $\bar{x} = \hat{\tilde{x}}$, the anti-automorphism with $\bar{v} = -v$ for $v \in V$.
obj.std-algebra.clifford-conjugation.technical: Clifford conjugation composes reversion with the grade involution. It is an anti-automorphism that negates vectors.
obj.std-algebra.clifford-conjugation.lay: Clifford conjugation reverses the order of products and also reverses every arrow, in the way that complex conjugation reverses the imaginary unit.

credit.name: Claude Opus 5.5
credit.source: Co-Authored-By trailer of the commit that added it

obj.std-algebra.clifford-group.technical: The twisted adjoint action sends $x$ to $\hat{g} x g^{-1}$; the grade involution on $g$ is what makes a single vector act as a reflection rather than as minus a reflection. The Clifford group consists of the invertible elements whose twisted adjoint action maps vectors to vectors. Products of invertible vectors, the versors, belong to it.
obj.std-algebra.clifford-group.lay: A versor is a product of invertible arrows. Each such product acts on arrows by sandwiching, and the action is a sequence of mirror reflections, one per factor.

credit.name: Claude Opus 5.5
credit.source: Co-Authored-By trailer of the commit that added it

obj.std-algebra.conformal-algebra.formal: For a nondegenerate real quadratic space $(V, Q)$ of signature $(p, q)$, the \emph{conformal space} is $V \perp H$ with $H$ a hyperbolic plane spanned by null vectors $n_0, n_\infty$ with $B(n_0, n_\infty) = -1$; it has signature $(p+1, q+1)$, and $\Cl(p+1, q+1)$ is the \emph{conformal algebra} of $V$. The \emph{conformal embedding} of points is $X(x) = n_0 + x + \tfrac12 Q(x)\, n_\infty$ for $x \in V$. The cases used in the store are $\Cl(4,1)$, the conformal algebra of Euclidean three-space, and $\Cl(2,4)$, the conformal algebra of spacetime $\R^{1,3}$.
obj.std-algebra.conformal-algebra.technical: The conformal algebra of a space adds one positive and one negative direction, written through two null vectors: the origin $n_0$ and the point at infinity $n_\infty$. A point $x$ is represented by the null vector $n_0 + x + \tfrac12 Q(x) n_\infty$. For spacetime this gives $\Cl(2,4)$, whose even part carries the twistors used in the series.
obj.std-algebra.conformal-algebra.lay: The conformal algebra adds two extra directions, one for the origin and one for "infinity". Points become special arrows of zero length, and spheres, planes and their transformations become simple elements of the algebra.

credit.name: Claude Opus 5.5
credit.source: Co-Authored-By trailer of the commit that added it

obj.std-algebra.even-subalgebra.formal: $\Cl^{+}(V, Q) = \bigoplus_{k \text{ even}} \Cl^{k}$ and $\Cl^{-}(V, Q) = \bigoplus_{k \text{ odd}} \Cl^{k}$. $\Cl^{+}$ is the \emph{even subalgebra}; its elements are \emph{even}, those of $\Cl^{-}$ \emph{odd}. They are the $+1$ and $-1$ eigenspaces of the grade involution.
obj.std-algebra.even-subalgebra.technical: The even part collects the even grades (scalars, bivectors, four-vectors, ...), the odd part the odd grades. The even part is closed under multiplication and is called the even subalgebra.
obj.std-algebra.even-subalgebra.lay: Elements built from an even number of arrows form a smaller algebra of their own, the even subalgebra. It is where rotations live.

credit.name: Claude Opus 5.5
credit.source: Co-Authored-By trailer of the commit that added it

obj.std-algebra.grade-involution.formal: The \emph{grade involution} $x \mapsto \hat{x}$ of $\Cl(V, Q)$ is $\Cl(-1_V)$, the automorphism extending the isometry $v \mapsto -v$ (\claimref{std-algebra.functoriality}).
obj.std-algebra.grade-involution.technical: The grade involution is the automorphism of the algebra that flips the sign of every vector. It exists and is unique because $v \mapsto -v$ preserves $Q$.
obj.std-algebra.grade-involution.lay: The grade involution reverses every arrow. Elements made of an even number of arrows are unchanged; those made of an odd number change sign.

credit.name: Claude Opus 5.5
credit.source: Co-Authored-By trailer of the commit that added it

obj.std-algebra.grade-projection.formal: For $v_1, \dots, v_k \in V$ the \emph{antisymmetrised product} is $[v_1, \dots, v_k] = \frac{1}{k!} \sum_{\sigma \in S_k} \operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\, v_{\sigma(1)} \cdots v_{\sigma(k)}$. The \emph{grade-$k$ subspace} $\Cl^{k}(V, Q)$ is the span of all antisymmetrised products of $k$ vectors ($\Cl^{0} = \R$). An element of $\Cl^{k}$ is a $k$-vector; a sum of $k$-vectors over several $k$ is a \emph{multivector}. By \claimref{std-algebra.grade-decomposition}, $\Cl(V, Q) = \bigoplus_{k=0}^{n} \Cl^{k}$, and $\langle x \rangle_k$ denotes the component of $x$ in $\Cl^{k}$, the \emph{grade-$k$ projection}. Grade $0$ is the \emph{scalar part}.
obj.std-algebra.grade-projection.technical: Grade is defined without choosing a basis: the grade-$k$ part of the algebra is spanned by the fully antisymmetrised products of $k$ vectors. For mutually orthogonal vectors the antisymmetrised product is just the product. The algebra is the direct sum of its grades, and $\langle x \rangle_k$ picks out the grade-$k$ component: scalars, vectors, bivectors and so on.
obj.std-algebra.grade-projection.lay: Elements of the algebra come in grades: numbers are grade zero, arrows grade one, oriented plane pieces grade two, oriented volumes grade three, and so on. Any element is a sum of parts of definite grade, and projecting picks out one of them.

credit.name: Claude Opus 5.5
credit.source: Co-Authored-By trailer of the commit that added it

obj.std-algebra.hyperbolic-plane.technical: A hyperbolic plane is a nondegenerate plane containing a null direction. Such a plane always has a basis of two null vectors $u$, $w$ normalised so that $uw + wu = 1$, a hyperbolic pair, and it is the plane $\R^{1,1}$ in disguise: $u + w$ squares to $1$ and $u - w$ to $-1$. This is the normalisation used throughout the series (for example in \claimref{primer.splitting-along-hyperbolic-plane}).
obj.std-algebra.hyperbolic-plane.lay: A hyperbolic plane is the simplest piece of space-time: one direction of space and one of time. Its two light-like directions, which have zero length, can be scaled so that they multiply together to give one. Every space with both space-like and time-like directions is built from such planes plus a part that is all space or all time.

credit.name: Claude Opus 5.5
credit.source: Co-Authored-By trailer of the commit that added it

obj.std-algebra.left-contraction.technical: The left contraction of an $r$-vector onto an $s$-vector is the grade $s - r$ part of their geometric product, and zero when $r > s$. It is the inner product used throughout the store; between two vectors it is the polar form. It differs from Doran and Lasenby's symmetric inner product only when the left factor has higher grade, or is a scalar.
obj.std-algebra.left-contraction.lay: Contracting an arrow onto a plane removes the arrow's direction from the plane, leaving the arrow in the plane perpendicular to it. Contraction is the opposite of the outer product: it takes directions away rather than adding them.

credit.name: Claude Opus 5.5
credit.source: Co-Authored-By trailer of the commit that added it

obj.std-algebra.minimal-left-ideal.formal: A \emph{left ideal} of $\Cl(V, Q)$ is a subspace $L$ with $\Cl(V, Q)\, L \subseteq L$; it is \emph{minimal} when $L \ne 0$ and its only left ideals inside it are $0$ and $L$. A \emph{spinor space} of $\Cl(V, Q)$ is a minimal left ideal $S$, carrying the \emph{spinor representation} $x \mapsto (s \mapsto x s)$; its elements are \emph{spinors}. For an idempotent $e$, $\Cl(V, Q)\, e$ is a left ideal; it is the spinor space generated by $e$ when it is minimal.
obj.std-algebra.minimal-left-ideal.technical: Spinors are defined inside the algebra: a spinor space is a minimal left ideal, a subspace closed under multiplication from the left that contains no smaller such subspace. The algebra acts on it by left multiplication. Ideals of the form $\Cl\, e$ with $e$ an idempotent are the usual source, as in the Fock space of \claimref{std-algebra.fock-representation}.
obj.std-algebra.minimal-left-ideal.lay: Spinors are usually introduced as columns of numbers acted on by matrices. Here they are elements of the algebra itself: a smallest subspace that the algebra maps into itself by multiplying from the left. No matrices need to be chosen.

credit.name: Claude Opus 5.5
credit.source: Co-Authored-By trailer of the commit that added it

obj.std-algebra.outer-product.technical: The outer product of an $r$-vector and an $s$-vector is the top-grade part, grade $r + s$, of their geometric product; it is extended to general multivectors by bilinearity. It is defined directly from the geometric product and the grade projection, so it lives in the same algebra.
obj.std-algebra.outer-product.lay: The outer product of two arrows is the oriented piece of plane they span; of an arrow and a plane, the oriented piece of volume. It keeps only the "new directions" part of the full product, and it vanishes when the factors share a direction.

credit.name: Claude Opus 5.5
credit.source: Co-Authored-By trailer of the commit that added it

obj.std-algebra.outermorphism.formal: For a linear map $f : V \to W$ between real quadratic spaces, its \emph{outermorphism} $\underline{f} : \Cl(V, Q) \to \Cl(W, Q')$ is the unique linear map with $\underline{f}(1) = 1$, $\underline{f}(v) = f(v)$ and $\underline{f}(X \wedge Y) = \underline{f}(X) \wedge \underline{f}(Y)$; through \claimref{std-algebra.exterior-isomorphism} it is $\Lambda f$. So $\underline{f}(v_1 \wedge \dots \wedge v_k) = f(v_1) \wedge \dots \wedge f(v_k)$, and $\underline{f}$ preserves grade. $f$ need not be an isometry.
obj.std-algebra.outermorphism.technical: Any linear map of vectors extends uniquely to a grade-preserving map of the whole algebra that respects the outer product: apply it to each factor of a blade. This is the outermorphism. Unlike the algebra homomorphism of an isometry, it is defined for every linear map, and it ignores the geometric product.
obj.std-algebra.outermorphism.lay: A linear map moves arrows. Its outermorphism moves planes, volumes and every other blade along with them, by moving each spanning arrow.

credit.name: Claude Opus 5.5
credit.source: Co-Authored-By trailer of the commit that added it

obj.std-algebra.pin-spin.technical: Pin is the group of products of unit vectors (vectors squaring to $\pm 1$), Spin its even part, and $\Spin^{+}$ the even products whose reverse-norm $R\tilde{R}$ is $+1$, equivalently those with an even number of negative-square factors. On the orthogonal side, $\mathrm{SO}^{+}$ is defined as the proper isometries built from an even number of reflections in negative-square vectors.
obj.std-algebra.pin-spin.lay: Pin and Spin are the groups of products of unit-length arrows. Spin keeps the products with an even number of factors; these act on space as rotations and boosts rather than mirror images.

credit.name: Claude Opus 5.5
credit.source: Co-Authored-By trailer of the commit that added it

obj.std-algebra.primitive-idempotent.formal: In a unital real algebra $A$, an \emph{idempotent} is an element $e$ with $e^{2} = e$. Idempotents $e, f$ are \emph{orthogonal} when $ef = fe = 0$; then $e + f$ is an idempotent. A nonzero idempotent is \emph{primitive} when it is not the sum of two nonzero orthogonal idempotents; equivalently, $0$ and $e$ are the only idempotents of the corner algebra $eAe$. A \emph{complete system} is a family of mutually orthogonal idempotents summing to $1$.
obj.std-algebra.primitive-idempotent.technical: An idempotent is an element equal to its own square, such as a projection. Two are orthogonal when both products vanish. A primitive idempotent cannot be split further into two orthogonal nonzero pieces, which is the same as saying its corner algebra $eAe$ has no idempotents besides $0$ and $e$. In a Clifford algebra, $\tfrac12(1 + u)$ is an idempotent for every $u$ with $u^{2} = 1$.
obj.std-algebra.primitive-idempotent.lay: An idempotent is an element that does nothing new when applied twice, like a projection onto a subspace. Primitive ones are the smallest such projections, and they are used to cut the algebra down to its spinors.

credit.name: Claude Opus 5.5
credit.source: Co-Authored-By trailer of the commit that added it

obj.std-algebra.projective-algebra.formal: The \emph{projective} (plane-based) algebra of Euclidean three-space is $\Cl(3,0,1)$, generated by $e_1, e_2, e_3$ with $e_i^{2} = 1$ and one null generator $e_0$ spanning the radical, $e_0^{2} = 0$. A plane $a_1 x_1 + a_2 x_2 + a_3 x_3 = \delta$ is the vector $a_1 e_1 + a_2 e_2 + a_3 e_3 - \delta e_0$; lines are bivectors and points are trivectors. The algebra is degenerate, and its even subalgebra contains the rotors and the translators $1 + \tfrac12 e_0 t$ of Euclidean motions.
obj.std-algebra.projective-algebra.technical: The projective algebra is a degenerate Clifford algebra: three Euclidean generators and one null generator that is orthogonal to everything. Vectors represent planes, and points are represented by trivectors. Rigid motions, translations included, are products in its even part. It is a standard example of a degenerate algebra used in practice.
obj.std-algebra.projective-algebra.lay: The projective algebra adds to ordinary space one direction of zero length that is perpendicular to everything. That extra direction lets translations be written as products, just as rotations are.

credit.name: Claude Opus 5.5
credit.source: Co-Authored-By trailer of the commit that added it

obj.std-algebra.pseudoscalar.formal: For $\R^{p,q,r}$ with its standard orthogonal basis, the \emph{unit pseudoscalar} is $I = e_1 e_2 \cdots e_n = e_1 \wedge \dots \wedge e_n$, written $\omega$ in \claimref{primer.sign} and \claimref{primer.centre}. $\Cl^{n}$ is one-dimensional, so every pseudoscalar of $\Cl(p, q, r)$ is a nonzero multiple of $I$; reordering the basis or reversing an axis changes $I$ by a sign.
obj.std-algebra.pseudoscalar.technical: The unit pseudoscalar is the product of the standard basis vectors in order: the oriented unit volume element of the whole space. The top grade is one-dimensional, so it is unique up to scale and its sign fixes an orientation.
obj.std-algebra.pseudoscalar.lay: The pseudoscalar is the oriented unit volume of the whole space. In three dimensions it is the unit cube with a handedness; in spacetime, the unit four-volume.

credit.name: Claude Opus 5.5
credit.source: Co-Authored-By trailer of the commit that added it

obj.std-algebra.quadratic-space.technical:
A real quadratic space is a finite-dimensional real vector space $V$ together with a quadratic form $Q$: a map with $Q(\lambda v) = \lambda^{2} Q(v)$ whose polarisation $B(u, v) = \tfrac12(Q(u+v) - Q(u) - Q(v))$ is bilinear. $B$ is the polar form. Degenerate forms are allowed: some nonzero vectors may be orthogonal to everything.

Orthogonality, null vectors and isometries are defined through $Q$ and $B$ in the usual way.
obj.std-algebra.quadratic-space.lay: A quadratic space is a space of arrows with a rule that assigns each arrow a number, its "square length". The rule may give negative numbers, as time directions do in relativity, and it may give zero for arrows that are not zero, as light rays do. Everything else in the algebra is built from this one rule.

credit.name: Claude Opus 5.5
credit.source: Co-Authored-By trailer of the commit that added it

obj.std-algebra.radical.technical: The radical of $(V, Q)$ is the subspace of vectors orthogonal to every vector, $\operatorname{rad} V = \{a : B(a, x) = 0 \ \forall x\}$. The space is nondegenerate exactly when the radical is zero. Radical vectors are null, since $Q(a) = B(a, a) = 0$; the converse fails, as a null vector need not be orthogonal to everything.
obj.std-algebra.radical.lay: The radical collects the directions that the length rule cannot see at all: they have zero length and are perpendicular to every direction. A space with no such directions is called nondegenerate. Degenerate spaces, where such directions exist, are where the Transport Papers do most of their work.

credit.name: Claude Opus 5.5
credit.source: Co-Authored-By trailer of the commit that added it

obj.std-algebra.reversion.formal: The \emph{reversion} $x \mapsto \tilde{x}$ of $\Cl(V, Q)$ is the unique anti-automorphism with $\tilde{v} = v$ for $v \in V$: $(v_1 \cdots v_k)^{\sim} = v_k \cdots v_1$. It is the homomorphism $\Cl(V, Q) \to \Cl(V, Q)^{\mathrm{op}}$ given by the universal property applied to $V \to \Cl(V, Q)^{\mathrm{op}}$.
obj.std-algebra.reversion.technical: Reversion reverses the order of every product of vectors and leaves vectors alone. It is an anti-automorphism, $(xy)^{\sim} = \tilde{y}\tilde{x}$, obtained from the universal property applied to the opposite algebra.
obj.std-algebra.reversion.lay: Reversion writes every product of arrows backwards. It is used to undo rotations: a rotation's reverse is its inverse.

credit.name: Claude Opus 5.5
credit.source: Co-Authored-By trailer of the commit that added it

obj.std-algebra.rotor.formal: A \emph{rotor} is an even versor $R$ with $R \tilde{R} = 1$. Rotors form a group under the geometric product, with $R^{-1} = \tilde{R}$, and act on $V$ by $x \mapsto R x \tilde{R}$ ($= \Ad_R(x)$, since $R$ is even). Scaled to unit factors, a rotor is an element of $\Spin^{+}(V, Q)$. The definition does not require $Q$ to be nondegenerate. \emph{Note (degenerate $Q$).} The group $\{R \in \Cl^{+} : R\tilde{R} = 1,\ R V \tilde{R} = V\}$ contains the rotors and can be larger when $Q$ is degenerate: in $\Cl(0,0,2)$ every vector is null, so the only versor is $1$, while $R = e^{f_1 f_2} = 1 + f_1 f_2$ is even, has $R\tilde{R} = 1$ and fixes every vector (\claimref{std-algebra.bivector-exponential-in-spin}(iii)). A statement about that larger group says so; a rotor is always an even versor.
obj.std-algebra.rotor.technical: A rotor is a product of an even number of invertible vectors whose reverse is its inverse. It acts on vectors by the two-sided sandwich $R x \tilde{R}$, which is an even number of reflections. The rotors are the group $\Spin^{+}$, and they make sense in degenerate algebras too, where they include translations. In a degenerate algebra the even elements with $R\tilde{R} = 1$ that map vectors to vectors can be more than the rotors: in $\Cl(0,0,2)$, where every vector is null, $1 + f_1 f_2$ is such an element but no product of invertible vectors.
obj.std-algebra.rotor.lay: A rotor is the algebra's way of encoding a rotation or a boost. It is a product of an even number of arrows, and applying it twice from both sides of an arrow turns the arrow. Undoing it means writing the product backwards.

The definition itself is unchanged.

credit.source: Co-Authored-By trailer of the commit that added it

obj.std-algebra.signature.formal: The \emph{signature} of a real quadratic space is the triple $(p, q, r)$ of the law of inertia, \claimref{std-algebra.sylvester-inertia}. $\R^{p,q,r}$ denotes $\R^{p+q+r}$ with the standard basis orthogonal and $Q(e_i) = 1$ for $i \le p$, $Q(e_i) = -1$ for $p < i \le p+q$, and $Q(e_i) = 0$ for the last $r$. We write $\R^{p,q} = \R^{p,q,0}$ and $n = p + q + r$. Every real quadratic space of signature $(p, q, r)$ is isometric to $\R^{p,q,r}$.
obj.std-algebra.signature.technical: The signature $(p, q, r)$ counts the basis vectors squaring to $+1$, $-1$ and $0$ in any orthogonal basis; it is well defined by the law of inertia. The model space $\R^{p,q,r}$ has an orthonormal standard basis with $p$ positive, $q$ negative and $r$ null generators, in that order, and represents every space of that signature.
obj.std-algebra.signature.lay: The signature is the triple of counts: how many directions square to plus one, to minus one, and to zero. Ordinary space is $(3, 0, 0)$; spacetime in the convention used here is $(1, 3, 0)$.

credit.name: Claude Opus 5.5
credit.source: Co-Authored-By trailer of the commit that added it

obj.std-algebra.spacetime-algebra.formal: The \emph{spacetime algebra} is $\Cl(1,3)$, the Clifford algebra of Minkowski space in signature $(+,-,-,-)$, with orthonormal basis $\gamma_0, \gamma_1, \gamma_2, \gamma_3$: $\gamma_0^{2} = 1$, $\gamma_k^{2} = -1$ for $k = 1, 2, 3$. Its pseudoscalar is $I = \gamma_0 \gamma_1 \gamma_2 \gamma_3$. For the observer with velocity $\gamma_0$, the \emph{spacetime split} assigns to $\gamma_k$ the \emph{relative vector} $\sigma_k = \gamma_k \gamma_0$, a bivector of $\Cl(1,3)$.
obj.std-algebra.spacetime-algebra.technical: The spacetime algebra is the Clifford algebra of Minkowski space with one positive and three negative directions, the store's convention. A frame $\gamma_\mu$ is the GA form of the Dirac matrices, but here the $\gamma_\mu$ are vectors, not matrices. An observer's time direction $\gamma_0$ turns each spatial vector into the bivector $\gamma_k \gamma_0$, which behaves as a vector of that observer's space.
obj.std-algebra.spacetime-algebra.lay: The spacetime algebra is the algebra of arrows in spacetime, one time direction and three space directions. An observer moving along the time direction sees space as the planes made by space directions with their own time direction.

credit.name: Claude Opus 5.5
credit.source: Co-Authored-By trailer of the commit that added it

obj.std-algebra.witt-index.formal: The \emph{Witt index} of a real quadratic space of signature $(p, q, r)$ is $m = \min(p, q)$, the number of hyperbolic planes in a Witt decomposition (\claimref{std-algebra.witt-decomposition}); it is the Witt index of the nondegenerate quotient $V / \operatorname{rad} V$. For nondegenerate $V$ it is the dimension of every maximal totally null subspace; in general maximal totally null subspaces have dimension $m + r$.
obj.std-algebra.witt-index.technical: The Witt index counts the hyperbolic planes in a Witt decomposition, $\min(p, q)$. In a nondegenerate space it is the largest dimension of a subspace on which the form vanishes identically; a radical adds its own dimension to that.
obj.std-algebra.witt-index.lay: The Witt index is the number of independent, mutually perpendicular light-like directions a space can hold. Ordinary space-time has Witt index one.

credit.source: Co-Authored-By trailer of the commit that added it

primer.centre.formal: For $n \geq 1$, the centre of $\Cl(p,q)$ is $\R \cdot 1$ if $n$ is even, and $\R \cdot 1 \oplus \R \cdot \omega$ if $n$ is odd, where $\omega = e_1 e_2 \cdots e_n$ is the pseudoscalar.
primer.centre.technical:
For $n = p + q \geq 1$, conjugation by a generator $e_j$ sends a grade-$k$ basis blade $e_I$ to $(-1)^{k - [j \in I]}\, e_I$, so a central element can only have components whose blades survive every such conjugation. For $0 < k < n$ a generator inside $I$ and one outside $I$ impose incompatible parity conditions, so the centre lies in $\R \oplus \R\,\omega$, and $\omega$ itself is central exactly when $n$ is odd.

Hence the centre of $\Cl(p,q)$ is $\R \cdot 1$ for even $n$ and $\R \cdot 1 \oplus \R \cdot \omega$ for odd $n$, with $\omega = e_1 \cdots e_n$ the pseudoscalar.
primer.centre.lay: The centre of an algebra is the set of its elements that commute with everything in it. For the Clifford algebra of a space with an even number of dimensions, only the ordinary numbers do this. With an odd number of dimensions there is one more such element, the product of all the basis directions, so the centre becomes two-dimensional.
primer.centre.typing_note: Self-contained proof in the source; no edges.

proofs.main:
For a basis blade $e_I$ of grade $k$ and a generator $e_j$, anticommuting $e_j$ through $e_I$ gives
\[
e_j e_I = (-1)^{k - [j \in I]}\, e_I e_j,
\]
where $[j \in I]$ is $1$ or $0$: passing $e_j$ across each factor of $e_I$ produces a sign except at the factor $e_j$ itself, if present. Every generator $e_j$ is invertible ($e_j^2 = \pm 1$), and conjugation by $e_j$ maps each basis blade to itself up to the sign above: $e_j\, e_I\, e_j^{-1} = (-1)^{k - [j \in I]}\, e_I$. A central element is fixed by every such conjugation, so each blade coefficient $\lambda_I \neq 0$ must have sign $+1$ against every $j$. Fix a blade $e_I$ with $\lambda_I \neq 0$ and $0 < k < n$, and choose $j \in I$ and $j' \notin I$ (possible since $0 < k < n$): the condition from $e_j$ is $(-1)^{k-1} = 1$ ($k$ odd), from $e_{j'}$ it is $(-1)^{k} = 1$ ($k$ even), and the two are incompatible. Hence $\lambda_I = 0$ for all $0 < k < n$, and any central $x$ lies in $\R \oplus \R\omega$. Finally $\omega$ itself: taking $k = n$, the condition from any $e_j$ (all $j \in I$) is $(-1)^{n-1} = 1$, i.e.\ $n$ odd. For $n$ even the centre is therefore $\R$; for $n$ odd, $\R \oplus \R\omega$.

primer.classification-real-clifford-alge.formal: Let $d \equiv p - q \pmod 8$. Then $\Cl(p,q)$ is isomorphic, as a real associative algebra, to the entry of the table of the section “The mod-8 classification”: $\Mat_k(\R)$ for $d \in \{0, 2\}$, $\Mat_k(\C)$ for $d \in \{3, 7\}$, $\Mat_k(\HH)$ for $d \in \{4, 6\}$, $\Mat_k(\R) \oplus \Mat_k(\R)$ for $d = 1$, and $\Mat_k(\HH) \oplus \Mat_k(\HH)$ for $d = 5$, with $k$ fixed in each case by $\dim_\R \Cl(p,q) = 2^n$. In particular $\Cl(p,q)$ is simple except when $p - q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, where it is the direct sum of two isomorphic simple algebras.
primer.classification-real-clifford-alge.technical:
The real Clifford algebra $\Cl(p,q)$ is, as a real associative algebra, a full matrix algebra over $\R$, $\C$ or $\HH$, or a direct sum of two copies of one, and which case occurs depends only on $d \equiv p - q \pmod 8$: $\Mat_k(\R)$ for $d = 0, 2$; $\Mat_k(\R) \oplus \Mat_k(\R)$ for $d = 1$; $\Mat_k(\C)$ for $d = 3, 7$; $\Mat_k(\HH)$ for $d = 4, 6$; and $\Mat_k(\HH) \oplus \Mat_k(\HH)$ for $d = 5$. The size $k$ is fixed by $\dim_\R \Cl(p,q) = 2^n$.

In particular $\Cl(p,q)$ is simple except when $p - q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, where it is the direct sum of two isomorphic simple algebras.
primer.classification-real-clifford-alge.lay: Clifford algebras built from a space with p positive and q negative directions turn out to be familiar objects in disguise: square tables of numbers whose entries are real numbers, complex numbers or quaternions, or a pair of such tables side by side. Which one appears depends only on p minus q, in a pattern that repeats every eight steps. The algebra splits into two identical pieces exactly when p minus q leaves remainder 1 on division by four.
primer.classification-real-clifford-alge.typing_note: Status left as proved, but the source's proof only points to the classical literature (ABS, Porteous, Lounesto) without repeating the induction; a reviewer may prefer status imported.

proofs.main: This is the theorem of the classical sources \cite{ABS1964, Porteous1995, Lounesto2001}, assembled from the low-dimensional isomorphisms of the section “The mod-8 classification” and the $(1,1)$-periodicity $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1) \cong \Mat_2(\Cl(p,q))$; we do not repeat their induction here.
proofs.via-periodicity: The table is part (iii) of \claimref{std-algebra.periodicity}. There the base cases $\Cl(k,0)$ and $\Cl(0,k)$ for $k \le 8$ are computed from the tensor rules, and every $\Cl(p,q)$ is reduced to one of them by $\Cl(p+1,q+1) \cong \Mat_2(\Cl(p,q))$ and by the period-eight rule $\Cl(p+8,q) \cong \Cl(p,q+8) \cong \Mat_{16}(\Cl(p,q))$. Reading the result by $p - q \bmod 8$ gives exactly the types stated here, with the matrix size fixed by the dimension $2^{p+q}$. This derivation supplies the induction that the main proof leaves to the reader.

primer.commutation-rule.technical: Let $v$ be a vector and let $x$ lie in the subalgebra generated by vectors orthogonal to $v$. Then $v\,x = \hat{x}\,v$ and $x\,v = v\,\hat{x}$, where $\hat{\cdot}$ is the grade involution. For a single orthogonal vector this is the anticommutation $vu = -uv$, and the general case follows because both sides are linear in $x$ and multiplicative, $\hat{\cdot}$ being an automorphism.
primer.commutation-rule.lay: In a Clifford algebra two perpendicular directions anticommute: swapping their order flips the sign. This rule extends that to anything built from directions perpendicular to a given one. Moving the given direction past such an element flips the sign of its odd part and leaves its even part alone.
primer.commutation-rule.typing_note: Self-contained proof in the source; no edges.

proofs.main: For a single orthogonal vector $u$ this is the anticommutation $vu = -uv = \hat{u}v$ of the section “Products of vectors, and the one rule”, and scalars commute with everything while being fixed by $\hat{\cdot}$. The general case follows because both sides of $vx = \hat{x}v$ are multiplicative in $x$ ($v(xy) = \hat{x}vy = \hat{x}\hat{y}v = \widehat{xy}\,v$, using that $\hat{\cdot}$ is an automorphism) and linear in $x$. The second identity is the first read from the other side, since $\hat{\cdot}$ is an involution.

__notes__.note.primer.abstract: This primer teaches the language of geometric algebra a reader needs before opening the Transport Papers. It motivates the geometric product from what the inner and cross products cannot do, compresses the answer into the one rule $v^{2} = Q(v)$, introduces blades and grades, explains what a signature is and why mixed signatures contain null vectors, presents the two canonical involutions, constructs rotors and the groups $\Pin$ and $\Spin$, and states the mod-8 classification of the real Clifford algebras. It then describes the conformal model, in which the oldest division by zero, $1/0$, is resolved by a projective completion. It closes with a toolkit that proves the classical structural lemmas the series imports: the commutation rule, the twisted adjoint action, the centre and pseudoscalar computations behind the classification (whose induction is cited, not repeated), and the splitting lemma. Every idea is introduced through a worked example, verified by machine in exact arithmetic. Each section names where the series uses its content, so the primer also serves as a reading route. The primer does not treat the failure of division: zero divisors, pseudo-inverses, and the taxonomy of obstructions are assigned entirely to T1, definitions and proofs alike. This is an expository companion, not a research contribution: nothing in it is new, and it carries no epistemic tier. For the mathematics developed properly, see the textbooks cited throughout; for the series' results, see T1, which restates each toolkit lemma it uses and cites this primer for the proof.
__notes__.note.primer.setting-what-primer-not:
The Transport Papers are a series about what happens where division fails in a Clifford algebra. The series' research papers hold themselves to a strict standard: complete proofs, declared hypotheses, machine verification. That standard leaves no room for slow explanations, and a reader meeting geometric algebra for the first time deserves slow explanations. This primer supplies them.

The plan is short. the section “Products of vectors, and the one rule” asks what a product of vectors ought to do, shows that the two products of ordinary vector algebra do not do it, and arrives at the geometric product and the single rule that generates it. the section “Blades and grades” shows what the resulting algebra looks like inside. the section “Signature, and the arrival of null vectors” explains signature, and why mixed signatures contain the null vectors that are the series' central subject. the section “The two involutions” introduces the two canonical involutions. the section “Rotors: how the algebra moves things” builds rotors, reflections, and the groups $\Pin$ and $\Spin$. the section “The mod-8 classification” states the mod-8 classification. the section “The conformal model, and the oldest division by zero” describes the conformal model and the oldest resolved division by zero. the section “The toolkit: the classical lemmas the series imports” collects, with complete proofs, the classical structural lemmas that T1 \cite{ButlerT1} imports. the section “Notation at a glance” is a one-page table of the symbols the series uses, for a reader who meets one before its section. the section “A reading route” is a reading route through the series. What happens where division fails, the question the series exists to answer, is deliberately not treated here: it is assigned to T1, and the section “Signature, and the arrival of null vectors” stops where that question begins. A reader who already works with the inner and outer products can begin at the section “Blades and grades” and use the section “Products of vectors, and the one rule” only to fix notation.

Three warnings, so that the primer is used correctly. First, it is bounded: no geometric calculus, no applications, no physics. The textbooks do all of that better \cite{Macdonald2010, DoranLasenby2003, DFM2007, HestenesSobczyk1984}. Second, the part used in the series' proofs is exactly one section: the research papers state every fact they use, and the toolkit of the section “The toolkit: the classical lemmas the series imports” is where the classical facts among them are proved (save the classification theorem, which the toolkit states with the classical sources cited for its induction). T1 restates the toolkit's lemmas, with their numbers here, and cites this primer for the proofs; everything before the toolkit is a convenience, so that a reader has an easy place to start. Third, it is not new: everything here is classical, and the classical sources are cited section by section \cite{Porteous1995, Lounesto2001, Lam2005, Chevalley1997, ABS1964}.
__notes__.note.primer.setting-products-vectors-one:
Adding vectors causes no trouble. Two displacements compose into a third, the picture and the algebra agree, and there is nothing to explain. What is wanted next is a product: a way of multiplying two vectors that is associative, that keeps the geometry of the pair, and that can be undone, so that knowing $a$ and the product $ab$ recovers $b$. Multiplication and division of vectors, on the same footing as multiplication and division of numbers. That is the whole demand, and it is worth being precise about how the products a reader already knows fall short of it, because the geometric product is built to repair exactly those faults.

Ordinary vector algebra in three dimensions offers two products. The inner product $a \cdot b = |a|\,|b| \cos\theta$ returns a number. It knows lengths and angles, which is most of Euclidean geometry, but it is symmetric in its two arguments and retains nothing about the plane they span. The cross product $a \times b$ returns a vector perpendicular to both, of length $|a|\,|b| \sin\theta$. It does record that plane, but it records it by pointing away from it, and that device is available in three dimensions only: in a plane there is no perpendicular direction to point along, and in four dimensions there are too many, since the vectors orthogonal to a given pair form a plane rather than a line.

Both products have a second limitation, and for this series it is the decisive one. Neither can be undone. Knowing $a$ and the number $a \cdot b$ does not determine $b$, and knowing $a$ and the vector $a \times b$ does not either. There is no division, and no candidate for one. A subject whose question is what happens where division fails cannot start there.

\textbf{What each product throws away, the other keeps.} The inner product keeps the cosine and discards the plane; the cross product keeps the plane and the sine. Each fails to be invertible exactly where it returns zero, and they return zero in complementary places: $a \cdot b$ vanishes when $b$ is perpendicular to $a$, $a \times b$ when $b$ is parallel to it, and for $a \neq 0$ both vanish only when $b = 0$. Between them they hold everything about the pair. So a single product that carried both pieces at once, the number and the plane, would have lost nothing, and would have a chance of being invertible. That is the product to build, and two questions stand in the way. What should record the plane of $a$ and $b$ in dimensions above three, where no perpendicular vector is available to stand in for it? And what does it mean to add a plane element to a number?

\textbf{The outer product answers the first.} Grassmann's answer, published in 1844, was to let the plane element be the object itself rather than a perpendicular substitute for it. The \emph{outer product} $a \wedge b$ is the oriented parallelogram spanned by $a$ and $b$: a plane, an area $|a|\,|b| \sin\theta$, and a sense of circulation around it. Exchanging the factors reverses that sense, so the product is antisymmetric,
\[
a \wedge b \;=\; -\, b \wedge a , \qquad \text{and in particular} \qquad a \wedge a \;=\; 0 .
\]
Only the plane, the area and the sense are recorded, not the particular parallelogram: $a \wedge (b + \lambda a) = a \wedge b$ for every scalar $\lambda$, so sliding one edge along the other changes nothing. Because the definition never mentions a perpendicular direction, it makes sense in every dimension. The object it produces is a \emph{bivector}, and it is not a vector. In three dimensions a bivector carries the same information as $a \times b$, which is why the cross product serves so well there, and why it does not generalise.

The construction does not stop at two vectors. The outer product is associative, so three vectors give $a \wedge b \wedge c$, the oriented parallelepiped they span: a three-dimensional subspace, the volume of that parallelepiped, and a handedness. That object is a \emph{trivector}. Four vectors give an oriented four-dimensional volume, and so on, the outer product of $k$ independent vectors representing the oriented $k$-dimensional subspace they span, weighted by its $k$-dimensional content. The antisymmetry that gave $a \wedge a = 0$ makes the outer product of any linearly dependent set vanish, so in an $n$-dimensional space the sequence ends at $k = n$: scalars, vectors, bivectors, trivectors, and upward to a single top object with nothing above it. That ceiling is not a convention. It is the statement that any $n+1$ vectors of an $n$-dimensional space are dependent.

\textbf{Clifford's step answers the second.} Keep both parts, and add them:
\[
ab \;=\; a \cdot b \;+\; a \wedge b .
\]
The objection is immediate: a number and a plane element are different kinds of object, and adding them looks like a mistake. The sum claims nothing about numbers and areas being the same kind of thing. It is bookkeeping: the two parts are kept in one symbol because they travel together and the pair is more useful than the pieces, in the way a real part and an imaginary part are kept together in one complex number. Elements that combine objects of several kinds in this way are called \emph{multivectors}.

What the sum buys is division. Take $b = a$: the outer part vanishes, and the product of a vector with itself is the pure number $a \cdot a$, its squared length. So whenever that number is not zero the vector has a two-sided inverse,
\[
a^{-1} \;=\; \frac{a}{a \cdot a} ,
\]
which is what neither the inner nor the outer product could supply alone. Clifford, in 1878, joined Grassmann's outer product to Hamilton's quaternions in exactly this way, and the algebra that results is the subject of this primer.

\textbf{One rule generates all of it.} That last observation is also the definition. If the square of every vector is a number, then polarising recovers both products, so nothing is lost by taking the one statement as the axiom and deriving the rest.

Start with a real vector space $\mathbb{V}$ carrying a quadratic form $Q$, which assigns to each vector $v$ a number $Q(v)$, its squared length. The \emph{geometric product} is the associative product generated by the vectors of $\mathbb{V}$ subject to one rule:
\[
v^{2} \;=\; Q(v) \qquad \text{for every vector } v .
\]
A vector times itself is a scalar. Everything else follows from this rule and associativity, and the algebra it generates is the \emph{Clifford algebra} $\Cl(\mathbb{V}, Q)$, called the \emph{geometric algebra} of $(\mathbb{V}, Q)$ when one wants to emphasise the geometry.

The two products return at once. Replace $v$ by $a + b$ in the rule and expand:
\[
(a+b)^{2} = a^{2} + ab + ba + b^{2}, \qquad \text{so} \qquad ab + ba \;=\; 2\, a \cdot b ,
\]
where $a \cdot b = \tfrac12\bigl(Q(a+b) - Q(a) - Q(b)\bigr)$ is the inner product obtained by polarising $Q$. So the symmetric part of the geometric product is the inner product, and \emph{orthogonal vectors anticommute}: if $a \cdot b = 0$ then $ab = -ba$. The antisymmetric part is the outer product of a figure of the original,
\[
a \wedge b \;=\; \tfrac12 (ab - ba), \qquad \text{so that} \qquad ab \;=\; a \cdot b \;+\; a \wedge b ,
\]
which is the decomposition this section arrived at geometrically. The rule constrains only the symmetric half, so the antisymmetric half is new content rather than something the axiom fixes; and that this half is the outer product already defined, and not merely some antisymmetric quantity, is what Example \claimref{note.primer.euclidean-plane} checks, where it comes out as the signed area of the parallelogram times the unit bivector. The product of two vectors is a scalar plus a bivector, and the bivector represents the oriented plane the two vectors span, weighted by the area of their parallelogram.
__notes__.note.primer.euclidean-plane:
Let $e_1, e_2$ be an orthonormal basis of the Euclidean plane: $e_1^{2} = e_2^{2} = 1$ and $e_1 \cdot e_2 = 0$, so $e_1 e_2 = -e_2 e_1$. Multiply two general vectors $a = a_1 e_1 + a_2 e_2$ and $b = b_1 e_1 + b_2 e_2$:
\[
ab \;=\; (a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2) \;+\; (a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1)\, e_1 e_2 .
\]
The scalar part is the dot product; the coefficient of $e_1 e_2$ is the signed area. One product carries both. Now square the bivector:
\[
(e_1 e_2)^{2} \;=\; e_1 e_2 e_1 e_2 \;=\; - e_1 e_1 e_2 e_2 \;=\; -1 .
\]
The unit bivector of the Euclidean plane squares to $-1$. The even elements $\alpha + \beta\, e_1 e_2$ therefore multiply exactly like complex numbers: the complex plane is contained in the geometric algebra of the real plane, as its even half, and the imaginary unit is the plane's own unit of oriented area. The invertible product the plane has had since the eighteenth century, complex multiplication, is therefore not an ingredient of the construction but a consequence of it.
__notes__.note.primer.setting-products-vectors-one: \textbf{Where the series uses this.} Everywhere, usually without citation. The commutation rule $ab + ba = 2\,a\cdot b$ is the identity used most often in the proofs of T1, and the observation of Example \claimref{note.primer.euclidean-plane}, that familiar number systems are geometric algebras under another name, recurs at every scale of the series.
__notes__.note.primer.setting-blades-grades:
Fix an orthogonal basis $e_1, \dots, e_n$ of $\mathbb{V}$. Because orthogonal vectors anticommute and each $e_i^{2}$ is a scalar, any product of basis vectors can be reordered and reduced until each index appears at most once. The surviving products
\[
1, \quad e_i, \quad e_i e_j \ (i<j), \quad e_i e_j e_k \ (i<j<k), \quad \dots, \quad e_1 e_2 \cdots e_n
\]
are the \emph{basis blades}, and they form a linear basis of the algebra: one blade for each subset of the indices, hence
\[
\dim \Cl(\mathbb{V}, Q) \;=\; 2^{n} .
\]
This count holds even when $Q$ is degenerate \cite{Chevalley1997}, a fact the series needs exactly once, in an essential step of one of T1's proofs.

A blade built from $k$ distinct vectors has \emph{grade} $k$, and the grades are exactly the objects the section “Products of vectors, and the one rule” built: scalars are grade 0, vectors grade 1, the bivectors grade 2, the trivectors grade 3, and so on up to the single top blade $\omega = e_1 e_2 \cdots e_n$, the \emph{pseudoscalar}, which represents the oriented volume of the whole space and is the top element that section's dependence argument located. Grade is basis-independent \cite{Porteous1995}, so the algebra splits into graded pieces, one for each dimension of geometric object it can represent: points of measure, directions, planes, volumes, and so on up to the space itself. The geometric product moves between the grades; the inner and outer products of the section “Products of vectors, and the one rule” are its grade-lowering and grade-raising parts.
__notes__.note.primer.setting-blades-grades-2: \textbf{Where the series uses this.} The blade basis and the $2^{n}$ count are the combinatorial foundation of every dimension argument in T1, and the machine verification scripts of the whole series compute in exactly this basis, with exact rational coefficients.
__notes__.note.primer.setting-signature-arrival-nu:
Over the reals, a nondegenerate quadratic form can be brought to a diagonal shape in which $p$ basis vectors square to $+1$ and $q$ square to $-1$; the pair $(p,q)$ is the \emph{signature}, and it is an invariant (Sylvester's law \cite{Lam2005}). Write $\Cl(p,q)$ for the corresponding algebra. Euclidean space is $(n, 0)$; the spacetime of physics is $(1,3)$: one time direction of positive square, three space directions of negative square.

Signatures with $p, q \geq 1$ are called \emph{mixed}, and something qualitatively new happens there. Positive and negative squares can cancel:
\[
v \;=\; e_1 + e_n, \qquad v^{2} \;=\; e_1^{2} + e_n^{2} \;=\; 1 - 1 \;=\; 0 \qquad (e_1^2 = 1,\ e_n^2 = -1).
\]
(The cross terms $e_1 e_n + e_n e_1 = 2\,e_1 \cdot e_n$ vanish because the basis is orthogonal.) A nonzero vector whose square is zero is called \emph{null} (or isotropic). Null vectors fill a cone, the \emph{null cone}, and in spacetime that cone is the light cone: the null directions are the paths light takes. In a definite signature there are no null vectors at all; $Q(v) = 0$ forces $v = 0$.

A vector with $Q(v) \neq 0$ has the inverse $v^{-1} = v / Q(v)$, since $v\,(v/Q(v)) = v^2/Q(v) = 1$; a null vector has none, and what that failure means, and what can be done about it, is the series' opening question. This primer stops here: the failure of division, its taxonomy, and its repair are assigned to T1, from the first definition onward.
__notes__.note.primer.hyperbolic-plane:
The smallest mixed signature is $(1,1)$, the \emph{hyperbolic plane}, and it is the smallest unit from which the whole subject is built. Set
\[
v \;=\; \tfrac12 (e_1 + e_2), \qquad w \;=\; \tfrac12 (e_1 - e_2) \qquad (e_1^2 = 1,\ e_2^2 = -1).
\]
Then $v^{2} = w^{2} = 0$: both are null. But their cross terms survive:
\[
vw + wv \;=\; 2\, v\cdot w \;=\; 2\cdot\tfrac14\,(e_1 + e_2)\cdot(e_1 - e_2) \;=\; \tfrac12\bigl(Q(e_1) - Q(e_2)\bigr) \;=\; 1 .
\]
A pair of null vectors with $vw + wv = 1$ is a \emph{hyperbolic pair}, and it satisfies the identity
\[
v\,w\,v \;=\; (1 - wv)\,v \;=\; v - w v^2 \;=\; v .
\]
Multiplying by $v$, then $w$, then $v$ returns $v$ exactly. What this identity means for the failure of division is the opening theme of T1; here it is simply an exact computation worth checking by hand.
__notes__.note.primer.setting-signature-arrival-nu: \textbf{Where the series uses this.} The null cone is the series' central object. T1 classifies what fails there and proves what repairs it; T5 applies the repair to the black-hole singularity, where spacetime's own light cones fold onto a single null direction; and the hyperbolic pair of Example \claimref{note.primer.hyperbolic-plane} reappears in T3 as a fermionic mode, one per rung of an infinite tower.
__notes__.note.primer.setting-two-involutions:
Two canonical symmetries act on every Clifford algebra, both fixed by what they do to vectors.

The \emph{grade involution} $x \mapsto \hat{x}$ sends every vector to its negative, $\hat{v} = -v$, and extends multiplicatively: $\widehat{xy} = \hat{x}\hat{y}$. On a blade of grade $k$ it gives the sign $(-1)^{k}$, so it fixes the even grades and negates the odd ones. It is the algebraic counterpart of the point reflection $x \mapsto -x$.

The \emph{reversion} $x \mapsto \tilde{x}$ fixes every vector, $\tilde{v} = v$, but reverses the order of products: $\widetilde{xy} = \tilde{y}\tilde{x}$. On a blade of grade $k$ it gives the sign $(-1)^{k(k-1)/2}$, the sign produced by reversing $k$ anticommuting factors. It plays the role that transposition plays for matrices and conjugation plays for complex numbers.

One consequence is used constantly. If a vector $v$ is orthogonal to every vector appearing in an element $x$, then moving $v$ past $x$ produces exactly a grade involution:
\[
v\,x \;=\; \hat{x}\,v .
\]
For a single orthogonal vector this is just anticommutation; the general case follows because both sides are multiplicative in $x$.
__notes__.note.primer.setting-two-involutions-2: \textbf{Where the series uses this.} The commutation rule above is applied dozens of times in T1's proofs, where it is equation (1); the grade involution is the symmetry whose innerness or outerness decides what happens to the split algebras in T1's fusion theorem; and reversion defines the rotor normalisation of the section “Rotors: how the algebra moves things”.
__notes__.note.primer.rotation-exactly:
In the Euclidean plane of Example \claimref{note.primer.euclidean-plane}, take $R = a - b\,e_1 e_2$ with $a, b$ real, not both zero (a rotor once normalised by $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$; the conjugation below ignores the scale). Its reverse is $\tilde{R} = a + b\, e_1 e_2$ and $R\tilde{R} = a^{2} + b^{2}$, so $R^{-1} = \tilde{R}/(a^2 + b^2)$. Conjugating $e_1$:
\[
R\, e_1\, R^{-1} \;=\; \frac{a^{2} - b^{2}}{a^{2} + b^{2}}\, e_1 \;+\; \frac{2ab}{a^{2} + b^{2}}\, e_2 .
\]
The coefficients are the cosine and sine of the double angle of the point $(a,b)$: the rotor rotates $e_1$ towards $e_2$ by $2\arctan(b/a)$, and with $a, b$ rational every entry is exactly rational. (The sign in $R$ is the usual half-angle convention, $R = \cos\tfrac{\theta}{2} - \sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}\, e_1 e_2$; the sign is easy to get wrong, and the machine check below verifies it.) This is the half-angle representation of rotations, and it is why rotors, like quaternions, cover the rotation group twice: $R$ and $-R$ rotate identically.
__notes__.note.primer.boost-what-it-does-null-dire:
In the hyperbolic plane $\Cl(1,1)$, even elements $R = a + b\, e_1 e_2$ have $R\tilde R = a^2 - b^2$, so rotors satisfy $a^{2} - b^{2} = 1$: they are the \emph{boosts}, the hyperbolic rotations of special relativity. Conjugating the null vector $v = \tfrac12(e_1 + e_2)$ of Example \claimref{note.primer.hyperbolic-plane}:
\[
R\,v\,R^{-1} \;=\; (a - b)^{2}\, v \qquad \text{(exactly, using } (a-b)(a+b) = 1\text{)}.
\]
A boost does not move the null direction; it \emph{rescales} it. The null lines are the boost's eigendirections, with reciprocal eigenvalues $(a \mp b)^{2}$. This one computation underlies a great deal of physics: it is why horizons redshift, and in the series it is why the completed algebra at a black-hole singularity carries a preferred one-parameter flow.

__notes__.note.primer.setting-mod-8-classification:
Every real Clifford algebra is a matrix algebra, or a pair of matrix algebras, over $\R$, $\C$ or $\HH$, and which one depends only on $p - q$ modulo 8 \cite{ABS1964, Porteous1995, Lounesto2001}:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{cl@{\qquad}cl}
\toprule
$p-q \bmod 8$ & type & $p-q \bmod 8$ & type \\
\midrule
$0$ & $\Mat_k(\R)$              & $4$ & $\Mat_k(\HH)$ \\
$1$ & $\Mat_k(\R) \oplus \Mat_k(\R)$ & $5$ & $\Mat_k(\HH) \oplus \Mat_k(\HH)$ \\
$2$ & $\Mat_k(\R)$              & $6$ & $\Mat_k(\HH)$ \\
$3$ & $\Mat_k(\C)$              & $7$ & $\Mat_k(\C)$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\noindent In each case the matrix size $k$ is fixed by the dimension count $2^{n}$. The small algebras are worth knowing by name: $\Cl(1,0) \cong \R \oplus \R$ (residue 1, split), $\Cl(0,1) \cong \C$ (residue 7), $\Cl(2,0) \cong \Cl(1,1) \cong \Mat_2(\R)$ (residues 2 and 0), $\Cl(0,2) \cong \HH$ (residue 6), $\Cl(0,3) \cong \HH \oplus \HH$ (residue 5), and the spacetime algebra $\Cl(1,3) \cong \Mat_2(\HH)$ (residue 6). The doubled rows, residues 1 and 5, are the \emph{split} algebras, the ones that decompose into two ideals; what that means for division is T1's type-C case.

The table repeats with period 8, and the repetition has a mechanism: adding one $(+1)$ and one $(-1)$ direction at once leaves $p - q$ unchanged and doubles the matrix size,
\[
\Cl(p{+}1,\, q{+}1) \;\cong\; \Mat_2\bigl(\Cl(p,q)\bigr),
\]
the $(1,1)$-periodicity theorem. This matters here, because the added $(+1,-1)$ pair spans exactly a hyperbolic plane: the unit of Example \claimref{note.primer.hyperbolic-plane} is also the unit of the classification's own periodicity.

\textbf{Where the series uses this.} T1 imports the pieces of this table its theorems rest on (the proofs are in the section “The toolkit: the classical lemmas the series imports”), and turns the classification into a state machine, the mod-8 clock: its Rule 1 fixes the residue, its Rule 2 moves it off the split rows exactly once. The tower of T3 is the $(1,1)$-periodicity iterated, one hyperbolic plane, and one fermionic mode, per step.
__notes__.note.primer.setting-conformal-model-olde:
The final construction is the one the series turns into a principle. Take a quadratic space $(\mathbb{V}, Q)$ of signature $(p,q)$ and adjoin two extra directions $e_+, e_-$ with $e_+^{2} = +1$, $e_-^{2} = -1$: one hyperbolic plane, giving $\Cl(p{+}1, q{+}1)$. Out of the new plane build the null pair
\[
n_0 = \tfrac12(e_- - e_+), \qquad n_\infty = e_- + e_+ ,
\]
representing the origin and the point at infinity, and represent each point $x \in \mathbb{V}$ by the vector
\[
X(x) \;=\; n_0 + x + \tfrac12 Q(x)\, n_\infty .
\]
A short computation gives $X(x)^{2} = 0$: every point of the space is represented by a \emph{null} vector in the enlarged space, determined up to scale, so points become null rays on a quadric. The lift also remembers the geometry exactly, since $X(x) \cdot X(y) = -\tfrac12\,Q(x - y)$. This is the \emph{conformal model} of geometric algebra \cite{Hestenes2001, DFM2007, DoranLasenby2003}, and its power is that the conformal transformations of $\mathbb{V}$, inversions included, all become sandwich products in the enlarged algebra.

What this primer takes from the model is the oldest division by zero. Take the real line, $\mathbb{V} = \R$ with $Q(x) = x^{2}$. The reciprocal $x \mapsto 1/x$ fails at the origin. In the enlarged space, the quadric is a circle, the projective line $\R P^{1}$ in homogeneous coordinates $[\,x : s\,]$, and the reciprocal becomes the linear swap $[\,x : s\,] \mapsto [\,s : x\,]$, which is total: it never fails anywhere. At the origin it gives $[\,0 : 1\,] \mapsto [\,1 : 0\,]$, the point at infinity. Division by zero has an answer; the answer simply is not a real number, and it lies in the completion. Nothing here is new: this is the nineteenth-century projective resolution of $1/0$, the same construction that makes M\"obius maps $z \mapsto (az+b)/(cz+d)$ total on the Riemann sphere.

What the series adds, and this is the point at which the reader should turn to T1, is a uniqueness claim: for a general quadratic space this completion is not one convenient construction among many but the \emph{unique minimal} resolution of the null cone's division failure, the repair of the element itself being provably impossible. The construction becomes a theorem.

\textbf{Where the series uses this.} T1 proves the uniqueness claim. T5 applies it to spacetime: the ascent $\Cl(1,3) \to \Cl(2,4)$ forced at the black-hole singularity lands on the conformal algebra of spacetime, whose spinors are Penrose's twistors (T9).

__notes__.note.primer.setting-rotors-how-algebra-m:
Geometric algebra does not act on vectors through matrices; it acts through its own elements, by a sandwich product. The basic case is the reflection. For an invertible vector $u$, the map
\[
x \;\longmapsto\; -\,u\,x\,u^{-1}
\]
is the reflection of the vector $x$ in the hyperplane orthogonal to $u$: it fixes everything orthogonal to $u$ (which anticommutes past $u$, absorbing the minus sign) and negates $u$ itself. Every isometry of a nondegenerate quadratic space is a product of reflections (the Cartan--Dieudonn\'e theorem \cite{Lam2005}), so products of invertible vectors, called \emph{versors}, reach every element of the orthogonal group $O(p,q)$.

The group formed by versors whose factors are normalised to $Q(u) = \pm 1$ is called $\Pin(p,q)$; its even part, products of an even number of unit vectors, is $\Spin(p,q)$, and covers the rotations. An even versor $R$ with $R\tilde{R} = 1$ is a \emph{rotor}, and it acts by plain conjugation, $x \mapsto R\,x\,R^{-1}$, two reflections making one rotation. One more name the series uses: $\Spin^0(p,q)$ is the \emph{identity component} of $\Spin(p,q)$, the elements joined to $1$ by a continuous path inside the group; in a definite signature of dimension at least two it is all of $\Spin$, while in mixed signature it is a proper subgroup. The precise action of a general versor, including the odd ones, needs a small twist by the grade involution; it is set out and proved in the toolkit (Lemma \claimref{primer.twisted-adjoint-action}).

__notes__.note.one-relation.two-presentations-diff: Proposition \claimref{one-relation.two-presentations} says that an orthogonal basis and a Witt basis generate the same algebra; this holds over every ring containing $\tfrac12$, and over the integers it fails. In $\Cl(1,1)$ let $e_{+}, e_{-}$ be orthonormal with $Q(e_{+}) = 1$, $Q(e_{-}) = -1$, and $a = \tfrac12(e_{+} + e_{-})$, $a' = \tfrac12(e_{+} - e_{-})$, so $a^{2} = a'^{2} = 0$ and $aa' + a'a = 1$. The integer span $\Lambda_{W}$ of the products of $a, a'$ is $\Z \oplus \Z a \oplus \Z a' \oplus \Z aa'$, and with $a, a', aa', a'a$ as the matrix units $E_{12}, E_{21}, E_{11}, E_{22}$ it is $\Mat_{2}(\Z)$, the integer form of Proposition \claimref{std-algebra.cl11-matrix}, with the integral idempotents $aa'$ and $a'a$. The integer span $\Lambda_{O}$ of the products of $e_{+}, e_{-}$ is $\Z \oplus \Z e_{+} \oplus \Z e_{-} \oplus \Z e_{+}e_{-}$, the matrices $\begin{psmallmatrix} \alpha & \beta \\ \gamma & \delta \end{psmallmatrix}$ with $\alpha \equiv \delta$ and $\beta \equiv \gamma \bmod 2$, a subring of index $4$ with $2\Lambda_{W} \subset \Lambda_{O}$, so $\Lambda_{O}[\tfrac12] = \Lambda_{W}[\tfrac12]$. Writing $x = \alpha + \beta e_{+} + \gamma e_{-} + \delta e_{+}e_{-}$, $x^{2} = (\alpha^{2} + \beta^{2} - \gamma^{2} + \delta^{2}) + 2\alpha(\beta e_{+} + \gamma e_{-} + \delta e_{+}e_{-})$, so every idempotent other than $0, 1$ has scalar part $\tfrac12$, and $\Lambda_{O}$, whose elements have integer scalar parts, has no idempotent other than $0$ and $1$; the idempotents $\tfrac12(1 \pm e_{+})$ of the orthogonal reading need $\tfrac12$. On the vector lattices the two presentations agree over $\Z[\tfrac12]$; over $\Z$ the null lattice $\Z a + \Z a'$, with $Q(xa + ya') = xy$ and the polar form $Q(u + v) - Q(u) - Q(v)$, is the even unimodular lattice $\mathrm{II}_{1,1}$ (the hyperbolic quadratic module, nonsingular), while the orthonormal lattice $\Z e_{+} + \Z e_{-}$, of index $2$ in it, is unimodular only for the half-polar form $B$, the odd lattice $\mathrm{I}_{1,1}$, and as a quadratic module it is singular at $2$ (polar determinant $-4$). So the metric chart and the CAR chart of the one relation are one object over the rationals and two different orders over the integers, and only the CAR chart contains the matrix units.

primer.sign.formal: $\displaystyle \omega^2 = (-1)^{\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}} (-1)^q = (-1)^{\tfrac{(p-q)(p-q-1)}{2}}$. In particular $\omega^2 = +1$ if and only if $p - q \equiv 0$ or $1 \pmod 4$.
primer.sign.technical:
For the pseudoscalar $\omega = e_1 \cdots e_n$ of $\Cl(p,q)$, with $n = p + q$, reversing the $n$ factors costs $(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}$, and $\omega$ times its reverse collapses to the product of the $Q(e_i)$, which is $(-1)^{q}$. Hence $\omega^{2} = (-1)^{n(n-1)/2}(-1)^{q}$.

A parity count shows this depends only on $p - q$: $\omega^{2} = (-1)^{(p-q)(p-q-1)/2}$, so $\omega^{2} = +1$ exactly when $p - q \equiv 0$ or $1 \pmod 4$.
primer.sign.lay: Multiplying all the basis directions of a Clifford algebra together gives a special element called the pseudoscalar. Its square is always plus one or minus one, and this result says which. The answer depends only on the number of positive directions minus the number of negative ones: plus one when that difference leaves remainder 0 or 1 on division by four, and minus one otherwise.

proofs.main:
Reversion reverses the factors of $\omega$, which takes $\binom{n}{2} = \tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$ transpositions of orthogonal (hence anticommuting) generators: $\tilde{\omega} = (-1)^{n(n-1)/2}\,\omega$. On the other hand $\omega \tilde{\omega} = e_1 \cdots e_n\, e_n \cdots e_1 = e_1^2 \cdots e_n^2 = (+1)^p(-1)^q$, collapsing from the inside out. Combining, $\omega^2 = (-1)^{n(n-1)/2}(-1)^q$. For the second form set $m = p - q$, so $n \equiv m \pmod 2$ and $q = (n-m)/2$; the exponent is
\[
\frac{n(n-1)}{2} + \frac{n-m}{2} \;=\; \frac{n^2 - m}{2},
\qquad
\frac{n^2 - m}{2} - \frac{m^2 - m}{2} \;=\; \frac{(n-m)(n+m)}{2} \;=\; 2pq,
\]
an even integer, so the exponent is congruent mod 2 to $\tfrac{m^2 - m}{2} = \tfrac{m(m-1)}{2}$. Hence $\omega^2 = (-1)^{m(m-1)/2}$, and $m(m-1)/2$ is even exactly for $m \equiv 0, 1 \pmod 4$.

primer.splitting-along-hyperbolic-plane.formal:
Let $\mathbb{V}' = H_0 \perp U'$ be an orthogonal decomposition of a real quadratic space, with $H_0$ a hyperbolic plane spanned by a hyperbolic pair $(v, w_0)$ (a pair of null vectors with $v w_0 + w_0 v = 1$, Example \claimref{note.primer.hyperbolic-plane}); the form on $U'$ may be degenerate. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\{1, v, w_0, v w_0\}$ is a linear basis of $\Cl(H_0)$, and every element of $\Cl(\mathbb{V}')$ admits a \emph{unique} expansion
\[
\sigma \;=\; \alpha + v\beta + w_0\gamma + v w_0\,\delta, \qquad \alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta \in \Cl(U').
\]
\item Left multiplication by $v$ is injective on $\Cl(U')$.
\end{enumerate}
primer.splitting-along-hyperbolic-plane.technical:
Let $\mathbb{V}' = H_0 \perp U'$, with $H_0$ a hyperbolic plane spanned by null vectors $v, w_0$ satisfying $v w_0 + w_0 v = 1$, and $U'$ carrying a possibly degenerate form. Then $\{1, v, w_0, v w_0\}$ is a basis of $\Cl(H_0)$, and every $\sigma \in \Cl(\mathbb{V}')$ has a unique expansion $\sigma = \alpha + v\beta + w_0\gamma + v w_0\,\delta$ with $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta \in \Cl(U')$; this is the graded tensor decomposition $\Cl(H_0 \perp U') \cong \Cl(H_0)\,\hat{\otimes}\,\Cl(U')$ in coordinates.

By uniqueness, left multiplication by $v$ is injective on $\Cl(U')$.
primer.splitting-along-hyperbolic-plane.lay: Suppose a geometry contains a special plane spanned by two zero-length directions. Then every element of its Clifford algebra can be written in exactly one way as four pieces, each a coefficient from the rest of the geometry multiplied by one of four simple elements of the plane. A consequence is that multiplying by one of the zero-length directions never destroys information carried by the rest of the geometry.

proofs.main:
(1) $\Cl(H_0)$ has dimension $4$; the elements $1, v, w_0$ are independent (grades $0$ and $1$), and $v w_0 = v \cdot w_0 + v \wedge w_0 = \tfrac12 + v \wedge w_0$ has a nonzero grade-$2$ component, so the four are a basis. Every vector of $U'$ is orthogonal to $H_0$, hence anticommutes with $v$ and $w_0$; consequently any product of generators of $\Cl(\mathbb{V}')$ can be reordered, changing only signs, into (an element of $\Cl(H_0)$)$\,\times\,$(an element of $\Cl(U')$). The products of the four basis elements of $\Cl(H_0)$ with the $2^{\dim U'}$ basis blades of $\Cl(U')$ therefore span $\Cl(\mathbb{V}')$, and since their number $4 \cdot 2^{\dim U'} = 2^{\dim \mathbb{V}'}$ equals $\dim \Cl(\mathbb{V}')$ (valid whether or not $Q'|_{U'}$ is degenerate, by the count of the section “Blades and grades” \cite{Chevalley1997}), they form a basis. This is the graded tensor decomposition $\Cl(A \perp B) \cong \Cl(A)\,\hat{\otimes}\,\Cl(B)$ \cite{Lam2005} in coordinates.

(2) For $x \in \Cl(U')$, the element $vx$ \emph{is} an expansion of the form in (1), with $\beta = x$ and $\alpha = \gamma = \delta = 0$. By uniqueness, $vx = 0$ forces $x = 0$.

primer.twisted-adjoint-action.technical:
For a versor $g = u_1 \cdots u_k$ set $\tau_g(x) = g x g^{-1}$ if $g$ is even and $\tau_g(x) = g \hat{x} g^{-1}$ if $g$ is odd. Each $\tau_g$ is an algebra automorphism, and on vectors it is the twisted adjoint $\Ad_g(x) = \hat{g} x g^{-1}$. For one invertible vector $u$,
$\Ad_u(x) = -u x u^{-1} = x - 2\,\frac{x \cdot u}{Q(u)}\,u$, the reflection in the hyperplane orthogonal to $u$.

With the Cartan-Dieudonné theorem, which writes every element of $\mathrm{O}(p,q)$ as a product of reflections, this makes $g \mapsto \Ad_g$ a map of $\Pin(p,q)$ onto $\mathrm{O}(p,q)$ with kernel $\{\pm 1\}$.
primer.twisted-adjoint-action.lay: Every symmetry of a geometry that preserves lengths can be built from mirror reflections. In a Clifford algebra each reflection is carried out by sandwiching with a single direction, and a product of directions carries out the combined symmetry. This result sets up the sandwich carefully, with a sign twist for products of an odd number of directions, and shows that each length-preserving symmetry comes from exactly two such products, differing by sign.

proofs.main:
For even $g$, $\tau_g$ is plain conjugation, an automorphism. For odd $g$,
\[
\tau_g(x)\,\tau_g(y) \;=\; g\hat{x}g^{-1}g\hat{y}g^{-1} \;=\; g\,\hat{x}\hat{y}\,g^{-1} \;=\; g\,\widehat{xy}\,g^{-1} \;=\; \tau_g(xy),
\]
and $\tau_g(1) = 1$, so $\tau_g$ is again an automorphism; naive conjugation by an odd versor is not vector-preserving, and the twist by $\hat{\cdot}$ is the standard repair. On a vector $x$, for odd $g$ we have $\hat{g} = -g$, so $\tau_g(x) = g\hat{x}g^{-1} = -gxg^{-1} = \hat{g}xg^{-1} = \Ad_g(x)$; for even $g$, $\hat{g} = g$ and the two agree at once. For a single invertible vector $u$, split $x = x_{\parallel} + x_{\perp}$ with $x_{\parallel} = \dfrac{x \cdot u}{Q(u)}\,u$ along $u$ and $x_{\perp}$ orthogonal to $u$: then $u x_{\parallel} u^{-1} = x_{\parallel}$ (parallel vectors commute) and $u x_{\perp} u^{-1} = -x_{\perp}$ (orthogonal vectors anticommute), so $-uxu^{-1} = x_{\perp} - x_{\parallel} = x - 2x_{\parallel}$, the stated reflection. Cartan--Dieudonn\'e \cite{Lam2005, Porteous1995} writes every element of $O(p,q)$ as a product of reflections, giving surjectivity; the kernel computation is classical \cite{Porteous1995}.

std-algebra.bivector-exponential.technical: When a bivector squares to a number, its exponential series collapses to two terms. A negative square gives the trigonometric form (a rotation), a positive square the hyperbolic form (a boost), and a zero square, a null bivector, gives exactly $1 + A$ (a null rotation, or a translation in a degenerate algebra). The exponential's reverse is its inverse, and for a simple bivector it is a product of two vectors, so it is a rotor.
std-algebra.bivector-exponential.lay: Turning by an angle in a plane is the exponential of the plane piece times the angle, just as $e^{i\theta}$ turns by $\theta$ in the complex plane. Planes whose square is positive give boosts instead of rotations, and planes containing a zero-length direction give the simplest motions of all, written exactly as one plus the plane piece.

proofs.main:
Powers follow from $A^{2} = \lambda$ by induction, and splitting the series into even and odd terms gives $\sum_k \lambda^{k}/(2k)! + A \sum_k \lambda^{k}/(2k+1)!$, which are the stated functions of $\theta$ (and $1 + A$ when $\lambda = 0$, the series terminating). The series converges absolutely in the finite-dimensional algebra. Reversion is a continuous anti-automorphism with $\tilde{A} = -A$ (\claimref{std-algebra.involution-properties}), so $(e^{A})^{\sim} = e^{-A}$, and $e^{A}e^{-A} = 1$ since $A$ commutes with $-A$.

Simple bivectors square to scalars. For vectors $a, b$, $a \wedge b = \tfrac12(ab - ba) = ab - B(a, b) = B(a, b) - ba$ by \claimref{std-algebra.product-decomposition} and \claimref{std-algebra.vector-squares}. Hence
\begin{equation}
(a \wedge b)^{2} = (ab - B)(B - ba) = B(ab + ba) - a\, b^{2} a - B^{2} = B(a, b)^{2} - Q(a) Q(b),
\end{equation}
using $ab + ba = 2B(a, b)$ and $a b^{2} a = Q(b) a^{2} = Q(a)Q(b)$; no orthogonal basis is needed. When $n \le 3$ every bivector is simple. By \claimref{std-algebra.exterior-isomorphism} the outer product is that of $\Lambda V$, which does not depend on $Q$, so it suffices that $\Lambda^{2} W$ is decomposable for $\dim W \le 3$. For $\dim W \le 2$ this is clear. For $\dim W = 3$ with basis $e_1, e_2, e_3$, write $\omega = x\, e_2 \wedge e_3 + y\, e_3 \wedge e_1 + z\, e_1 \wedge e_2$. If $z \ne 0$, then $\omega = (z e_1 - x e_3) \wedge (e_2 - \tfrac{y}{z} e_3)$, and the other cases follow by permuting the basis.

Rotors. Take $a$ with $Q(a) = \epsilon = \pm 1$ and $b$ orthogonal to $a$, and absorb the angle into $b$, so that $A = ab = a \wedge b$ (no normalisation of $b$) and $\lambda = A^{2} = -\epsilon Q(b)$ by \claimref{std-algebra.orthogonal-anticommute}. The exponential is $c + s\, ab$ with $(c, s) = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta/\theta)$, $(\cosh\theta, \sinh\theta/\theta)$ or $(1, 1)$. Then $c + s\, ab = a\,(\epsilon c\, a + s\, b)$ (since $a^{2} = \epsilon$ and $\epsilon^{2} = 1$): a product of two vectors. The second is invertible, since $Q(\epsilon c\, a + s\, b) = c^{2}\epsilon + s^{2} Q(b) = \epsilon(c^{2} - \lambda s^{2})$, which equals $\epsilon$ in all three cases ($\cos^{2} + \sin^{2}$, $\cosh^{2} - \sinh^{2}$, or $c = 1$, $\lambda = 0$). By \claimref{std-algebra.inverse-of-vector} both factors are invertible, so $e^{A}$ is an even versor with reverse-norm $1$, a rotor.
