std-algebra.radical-ideal-and-quotient.technical: In a Clifford algebra of a degenerate form the null directions orthogonal to everything, the radical, generate an ideal that is the same whether taken from the left, the right or both sides, because a radical vector anticommutes with every vector. In a basis split into a complement and the radical, the ideal is spanned by the blades with at least one radical factor; its $k$-th power by the blades with at least $k$ radical factors, so the $(r+1)$-th power vanishes and the $r$-th does not. Dividing out the ideal leaves the Clifford algebra of the nondegenerate quotient space, and the Clifford algebra of any complement is a subalgebra mapping onto it. The ideal is also the largest nilpotent ideal, identified intrinsically as the radical of the scalar-part form.
std-algebra.radical-ideal-and-quotient.lay: When some directions of a space have zero length and are perpendicular to everything, their algebra picks up a layer of elements that vanish when multiplied by themselves enough times. Removing that layer leaves exactly the ordinary algebra of the remaining, healthy directions, and that layer is the largest part of the algebra that both vanishes on repeated multiplication and is closed under multiplication by the whole algebra.

proofs.main:
Throughout, $B$ is the polar form of $Q$, and blades $e_I f_K$ are the increasing products in the basis $e_1, \dots, e_m, f_1, \dots, f_r$ of $V$; by \claimref{std-algebra.blade-basis} they form a basis of $\Cl(V, Q)$, degenerate forms included.

(i) For $f \in \operatorname{rad} V$ and $v \in V$, \claimref{std-algebra.vector-squares} gives $fv + vf = 2B(f, v) = 0$, so $f v = -v f$. For a product $a = v_1 \cdots v_k$ of vectors this gives $f a = (-1)^{k} a f = \hat{a} f$, and by linearity $f a = \hat{a} f$ for every $a$, since products of vectors span the algebra. Hence $a f c = a \hat{c} f \in \Cl\, \operatorname{rad} V$, so the two-sided ideal $J$ equals the left ideal $\Cl \operatorname{rad} V$, and by the same identity read the other way it equals the right ideal $\operatorname{rad} V\, \Cl$. Also $f^{2} = Q(f) = B(f, f) = 0$ and $f_i f_j = -f_j f_i$. A spanning set of $\Cl \operatorname{rad} V$ is $\{e_I f_K f_j\}$, and $e_I f_K f_j$ is $0$ if $j \in K$ and $\pm e_I f_{K \cup \{j\}}$ otherwise. So $J \subseteq \operatorname{span}\{e_I f_K : K \ne \emptyset\}$; conversely, if $K \ne \emptyset$ with largest index $k$, then $e_I f_K = (e_I f_{K \setminus \{k\}}) f_k \in J$. The blades with $K \ne \emptyset$ are independent, and there are $2^{n} - 2^{m}$ of them.

(ii) By (i), $J^{k}$ is spanned by products $a_1 f_{j_1} a_2 f_{j_2} \cdots a_k f_{j_k}$, and moving every radical factor to the right with $f a = \hat a f$ turns such a product into $\pm a_1 \hat a_2 \cdots f_{j_1} \cdots f_{j_k}$. The radical factors anticommute and square to zero, so the product of $k$ of them is $\pm f_K$ with $\lvert K \rvert = k$, or $0$. Hence $J^{k} \subseteq \Cl \cdot \operatorname{span}\{f_K : \lvert K \rvert = k\}$, which is the span of the blades $e_I f_L$ with $\lvert L \rvert \ge k$. Conversely such a blade is $(e_I f_{L'} f_{l_1}) f_{l_2} \cdots f_{l_k}$ with $l_1 < \dots < l_k$ the last $k$ indices of $L$, a product of $k$ elements of $J$. For $k = r + 1$ there is no such blade, so $J^{r+1} = 0$; for $k = r$ the blades are $e_I f_1 \cdots f_r$, nonzero by the blade basis, so the index is exactly $r + 1$ when $r \ge 1$.

(iii) $Q(v + f) = Q(v) + 2B(v, f) + Q(f) = Q(v)$ for $f \in \operatorname{rad} V$, so $\bar Q$ is well defined; its polar form is $\bar B(\bar u, \bar v) = B(u, v)$, and if $\bar u$ is orthogonal to all of $\bar V$ then $u \in \operatorname{rad} V$, so $\bar u = 0$: $\bar Q$ is nondegenerate. The map $v \mapsto \bar v \in \Cl(\bar V, \bar Q)$ satisfies $\bar v^{2} = \bar Q(\bar v) = Q(v)$, so the universal property (\claimref{std-algebra.existence-uniqueness}) gives a unique algebra homomorphism $\pi$ with $\pi(v) = \bar v$. It is onto since $\bar V$ generates. It kills $\operatorname{rad} V$, hence $J \subseteq \ker \pi$. The restriction $U \to \bar V$ is a linear bijection with $\bar Q(\bar u) = Q(u)$, an isometry of $(U, Q|_U)$ onto $(\bar V, \bar Q)$; so $(U, Q|_U)$ is nondegenerate, $\Cl(U, Q|_U)$ is the subalgebra of $\Cl(V, Q)$ spanned by the $e_I$ (\claimref{std-algebra.functoriality}), and $\pi$ maps it isomorphically onto $\Cl(\bar V, \bar Q)$ (\claimref{std-algebra.functoriality} again, both sides of dimension $2^{m}$). Counting, $\dim \Cl(V, Q)/J = 2^{n} - (2^{n} - 2^{m}) = 2^{m} = \dim \Cl(\bar V, \bar Q)$, so $\ker \pi = J$, and $\Cl(V, Q) = \Cl(U, Q|_U) \oplus J$ since the $e_I$ and the $e_I f_K$ ($K \ne \emptyset$) together form the blade basis.

(iv) Choose the basis of $U$ orthogonal with $Q(e_i) = \pm 1$, possible since $(U, Q|_U)$ is nondegenerate (\claimref{std-algebra.sylvester-inertia}). Left multiplication $L_x$ by a blade $x = e_I f_K \ne 1$ sends each blade to a multiple of a blade with a different index set (the symmetric difference with $I \cup K$), so its diagonal in the blade basis is zero; hence $\operatorname{tr} L_x = 2^{n} \langle x \rangle_0$ for every $x$. If $x$ is nilpotent so is $L_x$, and $\operatorname{tr} L_x = 0$, so $\langle x \rangle_0 = 0$. Let $N$ be a left ideal with $N^{k} = 0$. For $x \in N$ and any $y$, $yx \in N$ is nilpotent, so $\langle y x \rangle_0 = 0$ for all $y$. Take $y = e_I^{-1} = \pm e_I$ for $K = \emptyset$: since $e_I e_{I'} f_{K'}$ has scalar part $0$ unless $I' = I$ and $K' = \emptyset$, this reads off the coefficient of $e_I$ in $x$, which is therefore $0$; so $x \in J$ by (i). For right ideals use $\langle x y \rangle_0$ and $y = e_I^{-1}$ on the other side. Thus every nilpotent one-sided ideal lies in $J$, and $J$ is nilpotent by (ii). The same computation shows the radical of $(x, y) \mapsto \langle xy \rangle_0$ is exactly the span of the $e_I f_K$ with $K \ne \emptyset$, that is $J$: the blades pair diagonally, $\langle e_I f_K e_I f_K \rangle_0 = \pm\prod_{i \in I} Q(e_i) \prod_{k \in K} Q(f_k)$, which is $\pm 1$ for $K = \emptyset$ and $0$ otherwise. This description involves no choices. Applied with $r = 0$ it shows that $\Cl(\bar V, \bar Q)$ has no nonzero nilpotent one-sided ideal.

For $r = 1$, (ii) gives $J^{2} = 0$ and (i) gives $\dim J = 2^{n-1}$.

Example. Let $k \in \R^{1,3}$ be null and $U = k^{\perp}$, a three-dimensional subspace containing $k$. Every $a \in U$ has $B(a, k) = 0$, so $k \in \operatorname{rad} U$; choosing $e_1, e_2 \in U$ with $U = \R k \oplus \operatorname{span}(e_1, e_2)$, the form on $\operatorname{span}(e_1, e_2)$ is negative definite (a spacelike plane orthogonal to $k$), so $\operatorname{rad} U = \R k$ and $r = 1$. The inclusion $U \to \R^{1,3}$ extends to an injective homomorphism $\Cl(U) \to \Cl(1,3)$ (\claimref{std-algebra.functoriality}), so $\Cl(U)$ is the subalgebra generated by $U$. By (i) and (ii), $J = k\,\Cl(U) = \operatorname{span}\{k, k e_1, k e_2, k e_1 e_2\}$ with $J^{2} = 0$; its bivectors $N = k a$, $a \in \operatorname{span}(e_1, e_2)$, are the generators of the null rotations $1 + N$ about $k$: any two multiply to zero, so they commute, $N^{2} = 0$, and $e^{N} = 1 + N$ (\claimref{std-algebra.bivector-exponential}, null case). By (iii), $\Cl(U)/J \cong \Cl(\operatorname{span}(e_1, e_2)) \cong \Cl(0,2)$.

std-algebra.reflection.technical: Sandwiching a vector between a non-null vector $u$ and its inverse, with a minus sign, reflects it in the hyperplane perpendicular to $u$: the component along $u$ flips and the perpendicular part is untouched. This is an isometry with determinant $-1$, an involution, and it fixes every radical vector, since radical vectors are perpendicular to $u$. Two vectors of the same nonzero square are exchanged by the reflection in their difference when that difference is not null.
std-algebra.reflection.lay: Multiplying an arrow on both sides by a fixed arrow, with a sign, gives its mirror image in the plane perpendicular to the fixed arrow. This works for any fixed arrow that does not have zero length. Mirrors are the building blocks of all rotations.

proofs.main: Since $Q(u) \ne 0$, $x = \frac{B(x,u)}{Q(u)} u + x_{\perp}$ with $B(x_{\perp}, u) = 0$, which gives $V = \R u \oplus u^{\perp}$. By \claimref{std-algebra.inverse-of-vector}, $u^{-1} = u/Q(u)$. Then $u u u^{-1} = u$, and $u x_{\perp} = -x_{\perp} u$ by \claimref{std-algebra.orthogonal-anticommute}, so $u x_{\perp} u^{-1} = -x_{\perp}$. Hence $-u x u^{-1} = -\frac{B(x,u)}{Q(u)}u + x_{\perp} = x - 2\frac{B(x,u)}{Q(u)} u$. The right-hand side is a linear map fixing $u^{\perp}$ and negating $u$, so it is an involution with determinant $-1$; radical vectors lie in $u^{\perp}$. It is an isometry because $Q(-u x u^{-1}) = (u x u^{-1})^{2} = u x^{2} u^{-1} = Q(x)$ by \claimref{std-algebra.vector-squares}. It depends on $u$ only through the line $\R u$. Finally, with $d = a - b$, $B(a, d) = Q(a) - B(a, b) = \tfrac12 Q(d)$ because $Q(a) = Q(b)$, so $s_d(a) = a - d = b$.

std-algebra.rotors-beyond-exponentials.technical: Conjugating a vector by the exponential of a bivector is the exponential of the bivector's commutator action on vectors, a real linear map. The exponential of a real matrix can have a negative eigenvalue only from a pair of complex conjugate eigenvalues of the exponent, so every negative eigenvalue of such a conjugation comes with even multiplicity. In any signature with at least two positive and two negative directions, the rotor $R = -e_1e_2e_3e_4(\tfrac54 + \tfrac34 e_1e_3)$ acts on vectors with the simple eigenvalue $-4$ (a boost by the factor $4$ composed with the reversal of a $(2,2)$-plane), so neither $R$ nor $-R$ is an exponential. In dimension one and in $\Cl(1,1)$ the rotor $-1$ is not an exponential, although every rotor is plus or minus an exponential. Only one direction is shown: two positive and two negative directions suffice for a rotor that is not plus or minus an exponential; that fewer never allow one is not proved here.
std-algebra.rotors-beyond-exponentials.lay: Every rotation or boost written as the exponential of a plane element is an allowed rotor, but the converse can fail. One such rotor combines a boost with a half-turn of a four-dimensional block; the boost factor appears exactly once with a minus sign among the stretch factors, and an exponential can only produce such negative factors in pairs. The conformal algebra used for twistors, with two plus and four minus directions, is of this kind.

std-algebra.spin-double-cover.technical: Every isometry of a nondegenerate space comes from a product of unit vectors, and exactly two such products, $g$ and $-g$, give the same isometry. Even products give the isometries of determinant one; even products with $R\tilde{R} = 1$, the rotors, give the subgroup $\mathrm{SO}^{+}$. So each rotation or boost has exactly two rotors, $\pm R$.
std-algebra.spin-double-cover.lay: Every rotation, and every Lorentz boost, is produced by a rotor, and by exactly two of them, which differ by a sign. This two-to-one relation is the origin of spin one-half: a full turn of space changes the sign of the rotor.

proofs.main:
Homomorphism: $\Ad_{gh}(x) = \widehat{gh}\, x\, (gh)^{-1} = \hat{g}(\hat{h} x h^{-1}) g^{-1} = \Ad_g \Ad_h (x)$. For a unit vector $u$, $\Ad_u = s_u$ is a reflection (\claimref{primer.twisted-adjoint-action}, \claimref{std-algebra.reflection}) with determinant $-1$, so a versor of $k$ factors acts by an isometry of determinant $(-1)^{k}$.

Surjectivity: by \claimref{std-algebra.cartan-dieudonne} every isometry is $s_{u_1} \cdots s_{u_k}$ with $Q(u_i) \ne 0$; rescale $u_i$ to $Q(u_i) = \pm 1$ (allowed since $s_{\lambda u} = s_u$), so it is $\Ad_g$ with $g = u_1 \cdots u_k \in \Pin$. If it has determinant $1$ then $k$ is even and $g \in \Spin$. If moreover it lies in $\mathrm{SO}^{+}$, it has such a factorisation with $\prod Q(u_i) > 0$, so $g \tilde{g} = \prod Q(u_i) = 1$ (\claimref{std-algebra.inverse-of-vector}) and $g \in \Spin^{+}$.

Image of $\Spin^{+}$: if $R = u_1 \cdots u_k \in \Spin^{+}$, then $k$ is even, because a product of $k$ vectors lies in $\Cl^{k \bmod 2}$ and a nonzero element is not both even and odd (\claimref{std-algebra.z2-grading}); and $\prod Q(u_i) = R \tilde{R} = 1 > 0$. So $\Ad_R = s_{u_1} \cdots s_{u_k}$ is a product of evenly many reflections with $\prod Q(u_i) > 0$, which lies in $\mathrm{SO}^{+}$ by its definition.

Kernel: suppose $\Ad_g = 1$ on $V$ with $g \in \Pin$. By \claimref{std-algebra.z2-grading} a versor is even or odd. If $g$ is even, $g x = x g$ for all $x \in V$, so $g$ is central; by \claimref{primer.centre} the centre is $\R$ for $n$ even and $\R \oplus \R\omega$ for $n$ odd, and $\omega$ is then odd, so the even part of the centre is $\R$ and $g = \lambda$. If $g$ is odd, $g x = -x g$ for all $x \in V$; expand $g$ in an orthogonal basis of unit vectors. An odd blade $e_I$ commutes with $e_i$ for $i \in I$ (it passes $|I| - 1$ factors that anticommute and one that is $e_i$ itself) and anticommutes for $i \notin I$ (\claimref{std-algebra.orthogonal-anticommute}); conjugation by the invertible $e_i$ maps the blade basis to itself up to sign, so every blade of $g$ must anticommute with every $e_i$, forcing $I = \emptyset$, which is not odd. So $g = \lambda$, and $g\tilde{g} = \lambda^{2} = \pm 1$ gives $\lambda = \pm 1$. Conversely $\pm 1$ act trivially.

std-algebra.square-roots-of-minus-one.technical: How many essentially different square roots of $-1$ an algebra has depends only on its type. A real matrix algebra has them only in even size and then they are all alike; a complex matrix algebra has one class for each way of splitting the space into $+i$ and $-i$ eigenspaces; a quaternionic matrix algebra has exactly one class. Read through the classification of Clifford algebras this settles the question for every signature; the full classification for every $\Cl(p,q)$, with the centralisers, is in Hitzer, Ablamowicz and Sangwine.
std-algebra.square-roots-of-minus-one.lay: Many elements of a Clifford algebra square to minus one and so behave like the imaginary unit. In some algebras they are all the same up to a change of viewpoint; in others they come in a few distinct kinds. In the algebra of space-time they are all alike.

proofs.main:
$D = \C$: $f^{2} = -1$ means $f$ is annihilated by $x^{2} + 1$, which has distinct roots $\pm\mathrm{i}$, so $f$ is diagonalisable with eigenvalues in $\{\mathrm{i}, -\mathrm{i}\}$; it is conjugate to $\operatorname{diag}(\mathrm{i} 1_k, -\mathrm{i} 1_{m-k})$ with $k$ the dimension of the $\mathrm{i}$-eigenspace, which is a conjugation invariant.

$D = \R$: $f$ makes $\R^{m}$ a complex vector space with $\mathrm{i}$ acting as $f$, so $m = 2 \dim_\C$ is even; choosing a complex basis $b_1, \dots, b_{m/2}$, the real basis $b_1, f b_1, \dots$ puts $f$ in the standard block form $\operatorname{diag}(J, \dots, J)$ with $J = \begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}$. So all such $f$ are conjugate.

$D = \HH$: let $f$ act $\HH$-linearly on the right $\HH$-module $\HH^{m}$, and let $R_q$ be right multiplication by $q$. Then $f$ commutes with $R_{\mathrm{i}}$ and $(f R_{\mathrm{i}})^{2} = f^{2} R_{\mathrm{i}}^{2} = 1$, so $\HH^{m} = E_+ \oplus E_-$ with $E_\pm$ the $\pm 1$-eigenspaces of $f R_{\mathrm{i}}$. $R_{\mathrm{j}}$ commutes with $f$ and anticommutes with $R_{\mathrm{i}}$, so it exchanges $E_+$ and $E_-$, and $E_+$ is invariant under $R_{\mathrm{i}}$, a complex space of dimension $m$. A complex basis $b_1, \dots, b_m$ of $E_+$ is a quaternionic basis of $\HH^{m}$ (it spans $E_+ \oplus E_+ \mathrm{j} = E_+ \oplus E_-$), and on $E_+$, $f(b_k) \mathrm{i} = b_k$, so $f(b_k) = -b_k \mathrm{i}$. In this basis $f(\sum_k b_k q_k) = \sum_k b_k(-\mathrm{i}\, q_k)$: $f$ is left multiplication by $-\mathrm{i}$ on coordinates, $f = -\mathrm{i}\, 1_m$ as a matrix, the same for every $f$; so all $f$ are conjugate.

Sums: conjugation in $A \oplus A$ acts componentwise. The consequences follow from the table of \claimref{std-algebra.periodicity}: the real types $\Mat_m(\R)$ and $\Mat_m(\R)^{2}$ have $m = 1$ only for $\Cl(0,0) = \R$ and $\Cl(1,0) = \R^{2}$; $\Cl(1,3) \cong \Mat_2(\HH)$ and $I^{2} = -1$; in $\Cl(3,0)$ the centre is spanned by $1$ and $\omega$ (\claimref{std-algebra.complexification}), so $f \mapsto \langle f \omega^{-1}\rangle_0$ is a conjugation invariant, proportional to the complex trace's imaginary part, taking the values $1, -1, 0$ for $k = 2, 0, 1$.

std-algebra.sta-matrix.technical: In the store's signature the spacetime algebra is the algebra of $2 \times 2$ quaternion matrices, as the classification predicts for $p - q \equiv 6$. The familiar Dirac matrices are complex, so they represent the complexified algebra, $4 \times 4$ complex matrices; the real spacetime algebra sits inside as a real form. The spacetime split identifies the even part of the spacetime algebra with the algebra of the observer's three-dimensional space, and the two pseudoscalars coincide.
std-algebra.sta-matrix.lay: The algebra of spacetime arrows can be written with $2 \times 2$ arrays of quaternions, or, after allowing complex numbers, with the $4 \times 4$ Dirac matrices of relativistic quantum mechanics. Its even part is exactly the algebra of an observer's ordinary three-dimensional space.

std-algebra.sylvester-inertia.formal: Every real quadratic space $(V, Q)$ of dimension $n$ has an orthogonal basis $e_1, \dots, e_n$ with $Q(e_i) \in \{1, -1, 0\}$. The numbers $p$, $q$ and $r$ of basis vectors with $Q(e_i) = 1$, $-1$ and $0$ do not depend on the basis (Sylvester's law of inertia). Moreover $r = \dim \operatorname{rad} V$, and $p + q$ is the rank of any Gram matrix of $B$. Two real quadratic spaces are isometric if and only if they have the same $(p, q, r)$.
std-algebra.sylvester-inertia.technical: A real quadratic space always has an orthogonal basis in which every basis vector squares to $1$, $-1$ or $0$. How many of each, $(p, q, r)$, is the same for every such basis: this is Sylvester's law of inertia. The number of null basis vectors equals the dimension of the radical, and $p + q$ is the rank of the Gram matrix. The triple $(p, q, r)$ classifies the space up to isometry.
std-algebra.sylvester-inertia.lay: However you choose perpendicular unit directions in a space, you always find the same number of "space-like", "time-like" and "zero" directions. These three counts are the space's signature, and they are all there is to know about it.

std-algebra.tensor-rules.technical: A Clifford algebra of an orthogonal sum is a tensor product of the two algebras, provided one factor has even dimension and its vectors in the other factor are dressed with that factor's pseudoscalar. Dressing multiplies their squares by $\omega^{2}$, which is $+1$ for $\R^{1,1}$ and $-1$ for $\R^{2,0}$ and $\R^{0,2}$. So adding a hyperbolic plane doubles the matrix size, and adding a Euclidean or anti-Euclidean plane swaps the roles of $p$ and $q$. These rules drive the classification.
std-algebra.tensor-rules.lay: Adding two extra directions to a space has a predictable effect on its algebra: the new algebra is the old one combined with a small two-dimensional algebra, at the cost of possibly swapping which directions count as space-like and which as time-like. Repeating this explains why the algebras repeat with period eight.

proofs.main:
In the tensor product $\Cl(V) \otimes \Cl(W)$ the two factors commute. Since $\dim W$ is even, $\omega_W$ anticommutes with every $w \in W$, as distinct orthogonal vectors anticommute (\claimref{std-algebra.orthogonal-anticommute}) (\claimref{std-algebra.pseudoscalar-commutation}; directly, $w$ anticommutes with all but one factor of $\omega_W$ written in an orthogonal basis through $w$, and $\dim W - 1$ is odd). Put $\phi(v) = v \otimes \omega_W$ and $\phi(w) = 1 \otimes w$. Then $\phi(v)^{2} = v^{2} \otimes \omega_W^{2} = \epsilon Q(v)$, $\phi(w)^{2} = Q_W(w)$, and $\phi(v)\phi(w) = v \otimes \omega_W w = -v \otimes w\,\omega_W = -\phi(w)\phi(v)$. So $\phi(v + w)^{2} = \epsilon Q(v) + Q_W(w)$, and the universal property (\claimref{std-algebra.existence-uniqueness}) gives a homomorphism $\Phi$ from $\Cl(V \perp W, \epsilon Q \oplus Q_W)$. Its image contains $1 \otimes \Cl(W)$, hence $1 \otimes \omega_W^{-1} = \epsilon (1 \otimes \omega_W)$, hence $v \otimes 1 = \epsilon\,\phi(v)(1 \otimes \omega_W)$, so it is everything. Both algebras have dimension $2^{\dim V + \dim W}$ (\claimref{std-algebra.blade-basis}), so $\Phi$ is an isomorphism.

The signs: $\omega_W^{2} = (-1)^{k(k-1)/2} \prod Q(e_i)$ for an orthonormal basis of $W$ of dimension $k$ (\claimref{primer.sign}), which is $+1$ for $\R^{1,1}$, $-1$ for $\R^{2,0}$ and $\R^{0,2}$, and $+1$ for $\R^{0,8}$ and $\R^{8,0}$. With $\epsilon = -1$ the $p$ positive and $q$ negative vectors of $V$ become $p$ negative and $q$ positive ones. $\Cl(p,q) \otimes \Mat_2(\R) \cong \Mat_2(\Cl(p,q))$ is the matrix description of a tensor product with a matrix algebra, and $\Cl(1,1) \cong \Mat_2(\R)$ by \claimref{std-algebra.cl11-matrix}.

std-algebra.vector-squares.technical: A vector squares to its quadratic form, and the symmetrised product of two vectors is twice their polar form: $uv + vu = 2B(u, v)$. So the product of two vectors splits into the scalar $B(u, v)$ and the antisymmetric part $\tfrac12(uv - vu)$.
std-algebra.vector-squares.lay: Multiplying two arrows gives a number plus something new. The number is their ordinary dot product. The new part changes sign when the order is swapped, and turns out to be the oriented plane the two arrows span.

proofs.main: The first identity is the defining relation of \claimref{obj.std-algebra.clifford-algebra}. Applying it to $u + v$: $(u + v)^{2} = u^{2} + uv + vu + v^{2}$, so $uv + vu = Q(u + v) - Q(u) - Q(v) = 2B(u, v)$ by the definition of the polar form and \claimref{std-algebra.polarisation}. The splitting is $uv = \tfrac12(uv + vu) + \tfrac12(uv - vu)$.

std-algebra.witt-basis-car.technical: Pairs of null vectors with polar form one half between partners and zero otherwise satisfy, at the level of vectors and with nothing else assumed, the anticommutation relations of fermionic modes. Each hyperbolic plane supplies one such pair, $v = \tfrac12(e_+ + e_-)$ and $w = \tfrac12(e_+ - e_-)$. The number elements $w_i v_i$ are commuting projections. The algebra outside the pairs plays no role.
std-algebra.witt-basis-car.lay: Inside a Clifford algebra, a direction of space paired with a direction of time produces two zero-length arrows that obey exactly the rules for creating and destroying a fermion. With several such pairs you get several independent fermion modes, without building any Hilbert space first.

proofs.main: By \claimref{std-algebra.vector-squares}, $xy + yx = 2B(x, y)$ for vectors, which gives the three relations at once. Then $N_i^{2} = w_i v_i w_i v_i = w_i (1 - w_i v_i) v_i = w_i v_i - w_i^{2} v_i^{2} = N_i$ since $w_i^{2} = Q(w_i) = 0$. For $i \ne j$, $N_i$ and $N_j$ commute because each of $v_i, w_i$ anticommutes with each of $v_j, w_j$, and $N_i$, $N_j$ are products of two. $N_i + v_i w_i = w_i v_i + v_i w_i = 1$. For the hyperbolic planes: $Q(e_i \pm e_{k+i}) = 1 - 1 = 0$, $B(v_i, w_i) = \tfrac14(Q(e_i) - Q(e_{k+i})) = \tfrac12$, and vectors from different planes are orthogonal.

std-algebra.witt-decomposition.technical: In a nondegenerate plane, a null vector $u$ has exactly one partner $w$ with $uw + wu = 1$, so the plane is hyperbolic. Globally, a real quadratic space splits orthogonally into $\min(p, q)$ hyperbolic planes, a definite remainder and the radical. Taking one null vector from each hyperbolic plane, together with the radical, gives a totally null subspace of the largest possible dimension, $\min(p, q) + r$.
std-algebra.witt-decomposition.lay: Any space with both space-like and time-like directions can be cut into perpendicular copies of the simplest space-time plane, plus a leftover piece that is purely space-like or purely time-like, plus the directions the length rule cannot see. The number of space-time planes, the smaller of the two counts, is the largest number of independent mutually perpendicular light-like directions the space can hold.

proofs.main:
(i) Since $P$ is nondegenerate and $u \ne 0$, some $x \in P$ has $B(u, x) \ne 0$; rescale so that $B(u, x) = \tfrac12$. For $w = x + t u$ we have $Q(w) = Q(x) + 2t B(u, x) = Q(x) + t$ (by \claimref{std-algebra.polarisation}), so $t = -Q(x)$ makes $w$ null, and $B(u, w) = B(u, x) = \tfrac12$. By \claimref{std-algebra.vector-squares}, $uw + wu = 2B(u, w) = 1$. $u$ and $w$ are independent since $B(u, u) = 0 \ne B(u, w)$, so they span $P$. If $w'$ is another partner, $w' - w = s u + s' w$; nullity of $w'$ and $B(u, w') = \tfrac12$ give $s' = 0$ and then $s = 0$. With $e = u + w$, $f = u - w$: $Q(e) = 2B(u, w) = 1$, $Q(f) = -1$, $B(e, f) = Q(u) - Q(w) = 0$.

(ii) By \claimref{std-algebra.sylvester-inertia} take an orthogonal basis $e_1, \dots, e_p$, $f_1, \dots, f_q$, $z_1, \dots, z_r$ with $Q(e_i) = 1$, $Q(f_j) = -1$, $Q(z_k) = 0$. The $z_k$ are orthogonal to the whole basis, so they span $\operatorname{rad} V$. For $i \le m$ put $u_i = \tfrac12(e_i + f_i)$, $w_i = \tfrac12(e_i - f_i)$: both are null, $B(u_i, w_i) = \tfrac14(Q(e_i) - Q(f_i)) = \tfrac12$, and $H_i = \operatorname{span}(e_i, f_i)$ is a hyperbolic plane. The remaining $e_i$ or $f_j$ (only one kind remains) span a definite, hence anisotropic, $A$ of signature $(p - m, q - m, 0)$.

(iii) $N$ is totally null: the $u_i$ are null and mutually orthogonal, and the radical is orthogonal to everything. Its orthogonal complement is $N^{\perp} = N \oplus A$, since $B(w_i, u_i) \ne 0$ excludes the $w_i$ and nothing else is excluded. A null vector $x = n + a$ of $N^{\perp}$ has $Q(a) = Q(x) = 0$, so $a = 0$ and $x \in N$; hence no totally null subspace properly contains $N$. For the bound, let $T$ be totally null. $T$ meets the positive definite span $E$ of $e_1, \dots, e_p$ only in $0$, and the negative definite span $F$ of the $f_j$ only in $0$, so $\dim T \le n - p = q + r$ and $\dim T \le n - q = p + r$, that is $\dim T \le m + r$.

std-algebra.witt-extension.formal: Let $(V, Q)$ be a nondegenerate real quadratic space, $U \subseteq V$ any subspace and $f : U \to V$ an injective isometry. Then $f$ extends to an isometry of $V$, that is an element of $\mathrm{O}(V, Q)$. Equivalently (Witt cancellation): if $A \perp B$ and $A' \perp B'$ are nondegenerate with $A \cong A'$ and $A \perp B \cong A' \perp B'$, then $B \cong B'$. Every such extension is a product of reflections $x \mapsto x - 2\frac{B(x, a)}{Q(a)}\, a$, since $V$ is nondegenerate (\claimref{std-algebra.cartan-dieudonne}). The hypothesis that $V$ is nondegenerate cannot be dropped: an isometry of $V$ maps $\operatorname{rad} V$ to itself.
std-algebra.witt-extension.technical: In a nondegenerate quadratic space, any length-preserving embedding of a subspace, null or not, is the restriction of a global isometry. For a nondegenerate subspace the global isometry can be built from reflections one basis vector at a time. Over the reals cancellation also follows from the law of inertia. In a degenerate space the theorem fails, because isometries must preserve the radical.
std-algebra.witt-extension.lay: If two configurations of arrows have the same lengths and angles, some symmetry of the whole space carries one to the other. This holds even for configurations of light-like arrows, as long as the space has no invisible directions.

std-algebra.z2-grading.formal: $\Cl(V, Q) = \Cl^{+} \oplus \Cl^{-}$ with $\Cl^{i} \Cl^{j} \subseteq \Cl^{i+j}$ (indices mod $2$). So $\Cl^{+}$ is a subalgebra, of dimension $2^{n-1}$ for $n \ge 1$, and $\Cl^{-}$ is a $\Cl^{+}$-bimodule. More finely, $\Cl^{j}\Cl^{k} \subseteq \bigoplus_{m} \Cl^{|j-k| + 2m}$, $0 \le m \le \min(j,k)$.
std-algebra.z2-grading.technical: The algebra splits into even and odd parts, and products obey the parity rule: even times even is even, even times odd is odd, odd times odd is even. So the even part is a subalgebra of half the dimension. A product of a $j$-vector and a $k$-vector has grades from $|j - k|$ to $j + k$ in steps of two.
std-algebra.z2-grading.lay: Parity multiplies like signs: even with even or odd with odd gives even, mixed gives odd. A product of a $j$-grade and a $k$-grade element can only have grades between their difference and their sum, in steps of two.

proofs.main: $\Cl^{\pm}$ are the $\pm 1$ eigenspaces of the grade involution, an automorphism by \claimref{std-algebra.involution-properties}; if $\hat{x} = \epsilon x$ and $\hat{y} = \epsilon' y$ then $\widehat{xy} = \epsilon\epsilon' xy$. The dimension count is $\sum_{k \text{ even}} \binom{n}{k} = 2^{n-1}$ by \claimref{std-algebra.grade-decomposition}. For the finer statement take orthogonal basis blades $e_J$, $e_K$ with $|J| = j$, $|K| = k$: their product is a multiple of $e_{J \triangle K}$ and $|J \triangle K| = j + k - 2|J \cap K|$, with $|J \cap K|$ between $0$ and $\min(j, k)$ and $j + k - 2|J \cap K| \ge |j - k|$.

std-algebra.zero-divisors-annihilated.formal: Let $A = \Cl(V, Q)$ and $x \in A$. The following are equivalent: (a) $x$ is not invertible; (b) $xy = 0$ for some $y \ne 0$; (c) $yx = 0$ for some $y \ne 0$. If $(V, Q)$ is nondegenerate they are also equivalent to: (d) $xe = 0$ for a nonzero idempotent $e$; (e) $fx = 0$ for a nonzero idempotent $f$. For degenerate $(V, Q)$, (d) and (e) can fail: in $\Cl(0,0,1)$ the null generator $e_1$ is a zero divisor and $0$, $1$ are the only idempotents.
std-algebra.zero-divisors-annihilated.technical: In a finite-dimensional algebra an element fails to be invertible exactly when it kills something from one side, and then from the other side too. When the form is nondegenerate the Clifford algebra is semisimple, a matrix algebra or a sum of two, and then every element that kills something kills a nonzero idempotent: it annihilates a whole projection. With a degenerate form this fails, because nilpotent elements such as a null generator of the radical kill only other nilpotents.
std-algebra.zero-divisors-annihilated.lay: An element that cannot be divided by always destroys something when multiplied. In the algebras of nondegenerate spaces, what it destroys always includes a whole "projection", a piece of the algebra that behaves like a projector. In degenerate spaces this can fail: a zero-length direction perpendicular to everything destroys only things like itself.

proofs.main:
$A$ is finite-dimensional by \claimref{std-algebra.blade-basis}. Left multiplication $L_x$ is injective iff surjective. If $L_x$ is surjective there is $y$ with $xy = 1$; then $L_x L_y = 1$, so $L_y$ is injective, hence bijective, so $L_y L_x = 1$ and $yx = 1$: $x$ is invertible. Thus (a) $\Leftrightarrow$ $L_x$ not injective $\Leftrightarrow$ (b), and likewise with right multiplication for (c).

For nondegenerate $(V, Q)$, \claimref{primer.classification-real-clifford-algebras} gives $A \cong \Mat_k(D)$ or $\Mat_k(D) \oplus \Mat_k(D)$ with $D \in \{\R, \C, \HH\}$, a semisimple algebra. Under (b) the right annihilator $r(x) = \{y : xy = 0\}$ is a nonzero right ideal. In a semisimple algebra every right ideal has the form $eA$ with $e$ idempotent (Wedderburn-Artin: in $\Mat_k(D)$, a right ideal is the set of matrices whose columns lie in a subspace $U \subseteq D^{k}$, and $e$ is a projection onto $U$ along a complement; in a sum, componentwise). Then $e \in eA = r(x)$, $e \ne 0$, and $xe = 0$, giving (d); (d) implies (b). The left annihilator gives (e) the same way.

For $\Cl(0,0,1) = \R 1 \oplus \R e_1$ with $e_1^{2} = 0$: $(a + b e_1)^{2} = a^{2} + 2ab\, e_1$ equals $a + b e_1$ only for $(a, b) = (0, 0)$ or $(1, 0)$, and $e_1 e_1 = 0$.
